docs.title: Coxswain
docs.text:
Agents pull the oars. You hold the tiller. Coxswain is a platform that builds software with a crew of AI agents and keeps a person on the tiller: every change is planned, built under a budget, reviewed by two reviewers made to disagree, checked against the project's own tests, and handed to you as a pull request, with every stroke on the record. Coxswain is one repository and one package, coxswain, with one command, cox. Install it with brew install ppfenning/coxswain/cox or uv tool install --python 3.14 coxswain, then run cox install.

towpath, Coxswain's terminal home: the chair, the machines and every run on one screen.

docs.title: From 0.47 to the monorepo
docs.text: 0.47.0 was the last component release. 2026.10.0 is the first monorepo release. This page says what changed for you and how to move a machine across.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
One repository. Everything lives in ppfenning/coxswain. The tools, the graphs and harness, the cartridges and the crew are folders in it:

Folder Was src/tools coxswain-tools src/graphs coxswain-graphs src/cartridges coxswain-cartridges crew coxswain-crew

The component repositories get no further releases. coxswain-dash (towpath, Rust) stays its own repository and is still the optional --with dash.

One package. PyPI has one distribution, coxswain. It replaces coxswain-tools and the agent-cartridges uv tool. The command is still cox. The Homebrew formula is still cox in the ppfenning/coxswain tap.

One checkout per machine. A 0.47 machine had a checkout per component under ~/.local/share/coxswain/installs/ (coxswain-tools, coxswain-graphs, coxswain-cartridges, coxswain-crew) beside the coxswain checkout. Now there is one checkout, ~/.local/share/coxswain/installs/coxswain, with one venv at <checkout>/.venv. cox is installed editable from that checkout.

Team provider profiles live outside the checkout. The checkout ships the default provider profiles under src/cartridges/providers/. Your team's own profile, the one with its store, notifier and operator, lives in the workspace or in <home>/providers/, and the machine profile's provider_profile names it. See Install.

Crew is always linked. cox install and cox upgrade link the crew seats every time. There is no --with crew any more.

CalVer. Versions are YYYY.M.N: the year, the month, and a count of releases in that month, starting at 0. 2026.10.0 is the first; a November release would be 2026.11.0. The number says when a release was cut, not whether it is compatible. Compatibility is carried by the store and workspace schema and by cox setup migrate.

docs.title: Move a machine
docs.text:
Do this on each machine: the chair's machine and every lane host. Stop the chair loop and let the lanes on a machine finish before you move it.

  1. Drain the host, if it is in the hosts table and active.

    cox host drain <host>

    cox setup migrate --apply refuses an active host with migrate: refusing, host <host> holds active state, run cox host drain <host> first.

  2. Move a team provider profile out of the old cartridges checkout. If the profile's provider_profile names your team's own file inside installs/coxswain-cartridges, copy it (and catalog.yaml beside it) to <home>/providers/, then point provider_profile at the copy.

    mkdir -p <home>/providers
cp <home>/installs/coxswain-cartridges/providers/<team>.yaml <home>/providers/
cp <home>/installs/coxswain-cartridges/providers/catalog.yaml <home>/providers/

    Since 2026.10.1, migrate does the profile part itself when the cartridges checkout does not track your team's file: it copies the file to <home>/providers/ and points provider_profile at the copy. It does not copy catalog.yaml. A file it could not check against the checkout is left for you to move by hand. A profile outside the component checkouts is kept as it is.

  3. Update cox to the new package.

    brew upgrade cox

    Or, if you installed with uv, remove both old tools first. The agent-cartridges tool owns a cartridge executable, and the new package refuses to install over it.

    uv tool uninstall coxswain-tools agent-cartridges
uv tool install --python 3.14 'coxswain[postgres,traces,parquet,lake]'

    Name the extras this machine uses. A Postgres store needs postgres; the extras are traces, postgres, parquet, lake, analytics and live. --python 3.14 is needed when uv's default Python is older.

  4. See the plan. This changes nothing.

    cox setup migrate

    It prints one numbered line per step and ends with no changes made; run with --apply to migrate.

  5. Apply it.

    cox setup migrate --apply

  6. Edit your own scripts by hand. Migrate does not rewrite operator scripts, systemd units, drop-ins or launch agents that name an old checkout path. When this machine's state folder holds a migrate.json marker naming an old root, the apply lists them, one line each: migrate: <file> still names <path>; edit it by hand. It looks only in the home folder, ~/.config/systemd/user and its *.d drop-ins, ~/Library/LaunchAgents and the state folders, at .sh, .py, .zsh, .service, .timer, .plist and .conf files. Search anywhere else yourself, for example:

    grep -rlE 'installs/coxswain-(tools|graphs|cartridges|crew)' ~/bin ~/.config 2>/dev/null

  7. Check the machine, then put the host back to work.

    cox setup doctor
cox host activate <host>

  8. After every lane host has migrated, finish.

    cox setup migrate --finish
cox setup migrate --finish --apply

On the chair's machine, cox setup migrate --apply --hosts also runs cox setup migrate --apply on each lane host over ssh. Update cox on those hosts first. Without --hosts, the apply prints hosts: not touched; rerun with --apply --hosts on the chair's machine.

docs.title: Known issues in 2026.10.0
docs.text:
All three are fixed in 2026.10.1; they apply only to a migrate run with 2026.10.0.

  • repo_map written back in a form the profile reader rejects. The profile reader takes repo_map as one line of JSON. If a command then fails on that line, rewrite it as JSON: repo_map: {"<name>": "<path>"}.
  • Migration leases not always released. The apply takes a lease on each old checkout path. One left behind makes the next apply refuse with migrate: refusing, <holder> holds <path>. It expires an hour after it was taken; wait, then run the apply again.

  • A shallow 0.47 umbrella clone. If the coxswain checkout was cloned shallow, migrate may not find the release tag or may fail to sync. Fetch the tags and sync the checkout first, then run migrate again:

    git -C <home>/installs/coxswain fetch --tags
(cd <home>/installs/coxswain && uv sync)

docs.title: What cox setup migrate does
docs.text:
The plan comes from the machine as it is. In order:

  1. The coxswain checkout at installs/coxswain moves to the newest release tag (or --to VERSION). If it is missing, it is cloned at that tag.
  2. The checkout's venv is synced.
  3. Profile keys that name a component checkout move into the checkout: harness_dir to <checkout>/src/graphs, skills_roots and provider_profile under <checkout>/src/cartridges. A provider profile outside the component checkouts is your team's own and is kept. umbrella_dir is set to the checkout. A repo_map value that names a component checkout follows it to its retired folder.
  4. The workspace's cartridges/base and cartridges/local links are re-pointed at <checkout>/src/cartridges/cartridges/<name>.
  5. The Claude plugin marketplace is registered again at <checkout>/src/cartridges and its plugins reinstalled. When claude is not on PATH, this step is skipped and the plan says so.
  6. The coxswain-tools and agent-cartridges uv tools are uninstalled. coxswain is installed editable from the checkout with the extras the old tools had.
  7. A chair systemd unit, or a drop-in, whose PATH names a component checkout is rewritten.
  8. Each component checkout moves to installs/.retired-<date>/<name>, and its worktrees are repaired there. Nothing is deleted. Remove the retired folder yourself once you no longer need it.

After the steps, the apply prints a line for each of your own files that still names an old checkout (migrate: <file> still names <path>; edit it by hand), records a host beat, and ends with verify with: cox setup doctor.

A machine that has already moved plans one skip step, so running it again is safe.

docs.title: When it refuses
docs.text:
The plan refuses, and plans nothing else, when:

  • installs/coxswain is a file or a link, not a checkout;
  • the coxswain checkout has uncommitted changes (commit or stash first);
  • no release tag can be found to move to (pass --to);
  • the workspace cartridge links, or a component checkout's worktrees, could not be read.

--apply also takes a lease on each old checkout path, and refuses while this machine is busy:

  • another holder has one of those leases (migrate: refusing, <holder> holds <path>);
  • a live lane holds a run here;
  • the chair holds its lease here;
  • this host's row in the hosts table is active. Run cox host drain <name> first, and cox host activate <name> after the move.

Stop the loop and the lanes on a machine before you migrate it.

docs.title: What --finish does
docs.text:
--finish waits until this machine's plan is a single skip, its home checks pass, and every active host has reported a beat from the new layout. Until then it prints finish: waiting on ... lines.

It then finishes a move from an old checkout root outside the home, the layout installs used before 0.44.0. It rewrites the queue's repository paths under that root, removes the compatibility links left there, and deletes the migration marker. Without --apply it only prints what it would do.

If this machine never lived under such a root, there is nothing to finish: it prints finish: no old root known; pass --old-root.

docs.title: After the move
docs.text:
• Upgrade with brew upgrade cox (or uv tool upgrade coxswain), then cox upgrade.
  • cox versions shows the checkout's release and dash's tag against manifest.toml.
  • Each folder runs its own tests: cd src/tools && uv run pytest -q, and the same for src/graphs and src/cartridges.

See Install for a fresh machine and Releases for the version list.

docs.title: Release rehearsal gate
docs.text:
A release is cut only after a rehearsal has passed on the exact commit it is cut from: origin/main of the coxswain checkout. The rehearsal is a GitHub Actions workflow in the coxswain repository. You dispatch it; the release command only looks up its result. This page says how the pieces connect.

The rehearsal runs three scenarios. Each scenario is a job in the workflow, on a fresh debian:stable-slim container.

  • fresh: clone the repository into the default coxswain home, move the checkout to the candidate commit, install cox editable from it, run cox install --team rehearse --with dash, and check that cox setup doctor passes.
  • upgrade: install the previous release the way its own install page said, put real work items in a workspace, move the checkout to the candidate commit, run cox setup migrate --apply, and check that cox route lint still reads the work items. For a CalVer tag such as v2026.10.0 that is uv tool install --python 3.14 coxswain==2026.10.0, a clone of the tag, and cox install --with dash. For v0.47.0 it is the coxswain-tools package of the old multi-repository line, with --with crew --with dash.
  • migrate: the same start as upgrade, then run each migration the release declares against the workspace, linting after each one. The script runs a migration as cox migrate <id> --workspace <workspace>. cox has no migrate command yet, so a release that declares a migration fails this scenario until one exists; no release has declared one so far.

The scenarios are scripts/release_rehearsal.py. Each job installs git, curl, python3, uv, Node and Claude Code in the container, then runs the script with --scenario <name> and the four inputs. Every scenario ends by reading back the install: the checkout must be at the candidate commit and cox must be installed from that checkout. A green run therefore proves what its title names.

The migrate scenario may not skip when migrations are declared. It may skip only when the release declares none.

docs.title: 1. How the candidate reaches the workflow
docs.text:
The workflow is .github/workflows/release-rehearsal.yml. It runs on workflow_dispatch only. Everything it needs arrives as a dispatch input:

  • sha: the full 40 character commit SHA of coxswain.
  • dash_sha: the full SHA of coxswain-dash when the release tags dash; empty when dash keeps its pinned tag.
  • previous_tag: the last release tag, such as v2026.10.0. It feeds the upgrade and migrate scenarios. A v0.x tag is installed as the old coxswain-tools line; a CalVer tag as coxswain.
  • migrations: the declared migration list from section 2, as a comma separated string; empty when the release declares none.

A branch name or a short SHA is refused, because a branch can move between the rehearsal and the tag. Dispatch it from the coxswain checkout:

gh workflow run release-rehearsal.yml -f sha=$(git rev-parse origin/main) -f previous_tag=v2026.10.0 -f migrations=

Add -f dash_sha=<sha> when the release tags dash, and pass the declared migrations as -f migrations=<id>,<id>.

The workflow imports no release-command code. It does not read the manifest, the release notes or devtools. We chose inputs over a shared module so that the rehearsal tests what a user gets, not what the release tooling believes.

docs.title: A clean-machine rehearsal
docs.text:
The hosted run proves the scenarios on GitHub's runners. You can run the same scenarios on a machine of your own, in a throwaway container, before you dispatch. Start a fresh Debian container, install the same packages the workflow does, copy scripts/release_rehearsal.py in, and run it with the same inputs (--dash-sha and --migrations are optional):

apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates curl git python3 nodejs npm
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh && export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
python3 release_rehearsal.py --sha <sha> --previous-tag v2026.10.0

With no --scenario, the script runs all three and prints one result line each. Throw the container away afterwards. The release gate does not read this run; only the hosted run's title counts (section 3). It is extra evidence for the notes.

docs.title: 2. Where a release declares its migrations
docs.text:
A release declares its migrations in its release notes, not in the manifest. The notes are written once per release and read by the person who cuts it. The manifest outlives any one release, so a migration list there would go stale after the release ships.

The declaration is one line in docs/releases/<version>.md:

Migrations: <id>, <id>

Each id is a single token of letters, digits, hyphens and underscores. Ids are separated by a comma and one space. For example:

Migrations: split-lake-store, rename-slot-keys

The gate passes split-lake-store,rename-slot-keys as the migrations input.

An absent Migrations: line means the release has no migrations. The migrate scenario then skips. The line Migrations: none says the same thing out loud and is the preferred form. A Migrations: line with nothing after it is an unfinished edit, not a declaration. The gate refuses it, the same way it refuses an unwritten notes paragraph.

docs.title: 3. How the gate finds a passing run
docs.text:
The workflow sets its run name from every input that changes what is rehearsed: the coxswain SHA, dash's SHA, the previous tag and the migration list.

rehearsal sha=<sha> dash=<dash sha or pinned> previous=<tag> migrations=<list>

Each SHA is the full 40 character SHA; dash=pinned means the release keeps dash's tag. <tag> is the previous_tag input. <list> is the migrations input as passed, or none when that input is empty. The gate builds the same string from the checkout's origin/main commit (and dash's when the release tags dash), the previous release tag in the checkout and the Migrations: line in the notes. A run dispatched with a different previous tag or a different migration list therefore has a different title and never matches. The gate then lists dispatched runs of the workflow:

gh run list --workflow release-rehearsal.yml --event workflow_dispatch --limit 200 --json databaseId,displayTitle,conclusion,createdAt

The listing asks for 200 runs, because gh run list returns only 20 by default and a passing run could fall out of a short window. If the listing returns exactly 200 runs and none match, the gate says the window may be full instead of saying no rehearsal exists.

A run matches when its displayTitle equals the built string exactly. No prefix or substring match is used, so a run for one different input never matches. When several runs match, the gate uses the newest by createdAt. An older pass does not rescue a newer failure, and an older failure does not block a newer pass.

A run passes when its conclusion is success and the three scenario jobs fresh, upgrade and migrate are all present in its job list. The gate reads the jobs with gh run view <id> --json jobs. A missing scenario job fails the run. The fresh and upgrade jobs always apply, so each must have conclusion success. A skipped fresh or upgrade fails the gate, even when the run as a whole concludes success. Only migrate may be reported as a job with conclusion skipped, and a skipped migrate counts as present only when the release notes declare no migrations. When migrations are declared, migrate must have conclusion success.

If no run matches, or the newest match does not pass, the gate refuses and prints the run title it looked for.

docs.title: 4. How an override is recorded
docs.text:
An override lets a release go out without a passing rehearsal. It needs a named reason, given to the release command as --allow-no-rehearsal REASON. It is recorded in the release notes, in the ## Known gaps section, where the existing --allow-doc-drift override is recorded.

The existing override is free prose that the author writes by hand, and nothing in the release command reads the notes for it. The rehearsal override is stricter. It is one fixed line that the gate matches. The line is:

Cut with `--allow-no-rehearsal`: <reason>.

The reason says what was not rehearsed and why. For example:

Cut with `--allow-no-rehearsal`: the runner image was unavailable and the install path is unchanged since 2026.10.0.

The line starts with Cut with and the backtick-quoted flag, then a colon and one space, then the reason, then a final full stop. To compare reasons, the gate takes the text after the colon and space and before the final full stop, trims leading and trailing spaces from it, and tests it for equality with the trimmed command-line reason. A reason that itself ends in a full stop is written with that full stop followed by the line's own full stop.

The gate refuses an empty reason, and a reason that is only spaces. It also refuses when the notes lack the line, or carry a reason that differs from the one passed on the command line under that comparison. An override never waives a failed rehearsal silently. It replaces the lookup in section 3 and leaves a line in the notes that a reader can find.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
The parts of Coxswain. Four are folders of the one repository, ppfenning/coxswain, and ship in every release. Dash is its own repository and is optional.

Name Where Installed What it does Tools src/tools always, provides cox The cox CLI: install, dispatch, run the loop, land. Graphs src/graphs always The graphs a run executes, and the harness that runs them. Cartridges src/cartridges always A team's or repo's context: roles, skills, policy, providers. Crew crew always, linked into ~/.claude/agents The agent seats that plan, build, review, and validate. Dash ppfenning/coxswain-dash --with dash, provides towpath A terminal dashboard for the fleet.

The four folders are one checkout at one release tag, with one venv, so they always match. manifest.toml names only dash, at the tag a release pins it to.

Each folder runs its own tests from inside it:

cd src/tools && uv run pytest -q

The same works for src/graphs and src/cartridges. The root suite runs from the repository root with uv run pytest -q.

docs.title: Cartridges
docs.text: A cartridge is a packaged bundle of context for a team or a repo: its conventions, its charter, its thresholds. Cartridges are what let the same crew and the same graphs behave differently for different teams without changing any code.

docs.title: What it owns
docs.text: The src/cartridges folder holds the core package (merge, policy, ledger, work store), the base and local cartridges, the provider profiles, the reference skills plugins and the Claude plugin marketplace. See Cartridges for how a run picks one.

docs.title: Installing it
docs.text: Cartridges ships in every install. A workspace's cartridges/base and cartridges/local link into the checkout's src/cartridges/cartridges/. The shipped provider profiles are defaults in src/cartridges/providers/; a team's own profile lives outside the checkout, in the workspace or in <home>/providers/.

docs.title: Its own docs
docs.text: The folder's README and docs live at src/cartridges.

docs.title: cartridges
docs.text:
Who a run works for. This folder is the core package and the cartridge data inside the coxswain repository; it ships as part of the one coxswain package. To install Coxswain, see the root README.

Graphs reference abstract roles (plan, build, review_charter). A cartridge binds those roles to real skills, names where writes land, and carries the team's own written conventions. The same graph runs for any team that can fill the contract: swapping trackers, style charters or model providers is an edit to one file, not a rewrite.

docs.title: What is here
docs.text:
core/                pure substrate: merge, policy, manifest, ledger, work store, intake
cartridges/base/     the contract: roles, write-kind taxonomy, autonomy policy
cartridges/local/    the filesystem-only cartridge every install starts from
cartridges/<name>/   example-team, and the comfort presets local-comfort0 and local-comfort1
providers/           the shipped provider profiles (tier -> model) and catalog.yaml, the model price list
skills-plugins/      the reference `local-skills` plugin and the `coxswain` session plugin
context-templates/   starting points for a team's own context packs
.claude-plugin/      the Claude Code plugin marketplace, named coxswain-cartridges
docs/                design notes and the clean-room rule
tests/               this folder's suite

A workspace's cartridges/base and cartridges/local are links into cartridges/ here, so they move with the checkout's release.

docs.title: Provider profiles
docs.text:
A provider profile names the runner, maps each tier to a model, and sets the budget for each tier and role. The files in providers/ are the shipped defaults: claude-code.yaml, anthropic-default.yaml and local-oss.yaml. A fresh cox install points the machine profile's provider_profile at <checkout>/src/cartridges/providers/claude-code.yaml.

A profile your team edits is team configuration, not code. Keep it outside the checkout, in the workspace or in <home>/providers/, and point provider_profile in each machine's profile at it. An edited file inside the checkout makes it dirty, and cox upgrade refuses a dirty checkout. Copy catalog.yaml along with the profile: the chair reads model prices from the catalog.yaml beside provider_profile first. cox setup migrate leaves a profile that is already outside the checkout where it is.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
From this folder:

cd src/cartridges && uv run pytest -q

Fixtures are synthetic. The suite leans hardest on the ways autonomy must fail to be granted: streaks that do not transfer across kinds, risks, cartridge hashes or provider profiles, and a single reversal resetting the streak and doubling the bar.

docs.title: Working with a cartridge
docs.text:
Resolve and validate the local cartridge from this folder:

uv run python -m core.cartridge --team local --json --skills-root skills-plugins

--skills-root checks that every bound skill name resolves to exactly one skill body; pass it once per plugin root.

Start your own team's cartridge in your workspace:

cartridge init my-team --cartridges-dir <workspace>/cartridges

It creates my-team/, its context/ tree, links to base and local, and a cartridge.yaml naming the team. cox install registers the marketplace at <checkout>/src/cartridges and installs local-skills@coxswain-cartridges when claude is on PATH.

The docs site explains the rest: cartridges, team cartridge and policy, including how a write kind earns autonomy.

docs.text: MIT. See LICENSE.

docs.title: Crew
docs.text: The crew is the agents that do the rowing: they plan, build, review, and validate. The coxswain steers; the crew rows.

docs.title: What it owns
docs.text: The crew folder holds eleven seat definitions — recon, triage, build, review, ops, the board, writing, the scribe, the steward, the courier and the model steward — each one role filled by one agent doing one job.

docs.title: Installing it
docs.text: cox install and cox upgrade link every seat from <checkout>/crew into ~/.claude/agents. Nothing to pass.

docs.title: Its own docs
docs.text: The folder's README lives at crew.

docs.title: crew
docs.text:
A standing cast of named agent seats — who does what, what each may touch, and how each reports — with no employer inside any of them. This folder is part of the coxswain repository and ships in every release. To install Coxswain, see the root README.

Most agent rosters hardcode a workplace into the definitions: this tracker, that board, those conventions. Then the team changes, or you do, and the roster is worthless. Here the seat is the durable part and the employer is a binding you swap.

docs.title: What is here
docs.text:
seats/          one agent definition per seat (eleven), and SEATS.md for the chair
install.sh      links every seat into ~/.claude/agents (SEATS.md is not linked)
check_seats.py  checks every seat's frontmatter: name, description, tools, an explicit model

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
From this folder:

cd crew && python3 check_seats.py

docs.title: The cast
docs.text:
Three lanes, grouped by what a seat may touch rather than by who reports to whom. The read-only lane exists so findings arrive from eyes that did not do the work.

Seat Voice Surface Write authority Nova af_nova recon — codebase sweeps, log analysis, research, readiness audits none Sky af_sky triage and incidents — alerts, failures, blast radius none Lewis bm_lewis review — reads the diff, never the builder's account of it none, and no merge Sarah af_sarah build — worktree, branch, tests, one pull request code on its own branch Michael am_michael ops — CI, PR health, deploys, local tooling its own PR branches Emma bf_emma the board — epics, phases, item bodies, dates, reconciliation proposes; the chair writes Echo am_echo writing — docs, RFCs, outward-facing replies drafts only Alice bf_alice scribe — the visual plan for a swarm, tracked to completion plans/ only Daniel bm_daniel steward — reads the run records and proposes what should change: skills, workflows, spend, hygiene none; every change is a PR Liam am_liam courier — reads the courier inbox, resolves each reference, relays it to its owner none; acks only Model steward none declared model choice — owns which model each role runs on, read off the run stats; not daniel, who changes skills and workflows proposes, never applies; one weekly pull request to the provider profile

The chair is the session you are talking to, not a file: bare cox takes the chair lease for its session unless a live cox chair run loop, the same role run unattended, already holds it. seats/SEATS.md says why it has no seat file.

A reviewer is independent by construction. Lewis reads the diff and a base ref, never the builder's summary, and is never the instance that wrote the code. He advises — not ready, split this, close it instead — and merge stays human.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
cox install and cox upgrade run install.sh for you. To run it by hand from a checkout:

crew/install.sh            # symlink every seat into ~/.claude/agents
crew/install.sh --check    # what is installed, and from where

Symlinks, not copies, so editing a seat here changes what every session loads. --prefix DIR installs into DIR instead. A file that is not a symlink is never overwritten; install.sh says so and skips that seat. --uninstall removes only the links that point here.

docs.title: Binding a seat to your team
docs.text:
A seat names roles; a cartridge says which skills fill them. Add a cast: block to your team cartridge (see src/cartridges):

cast:
  nova:
    skills:   [audit-and-apply, pr-fleet-sweep]
    context:  "the read side of your internal SDK"
  sarah:
    skills:   [feature-lifecycle, test-driven-development]

Unbound seats still work; they simply route to nothing team-specific. Nothing in this repository names a company, a tracker, a board, or a person.

docs.title: Voice is decoration
docs.text: Every seat is a plain agent definition and works in any session. In a voice session a seat reports in its own voice, which is how you hear that a finding came from an independent pair of eyes rather than from the chair restating itself. In a text session the voice line is dropped. The model steward declares no voice. The other ten voices ship with Kokoro; none is required.

docs.title: Dash
docs.text: Dash is towpath, a terminal dashboard for the fleet: lanes, the chair, the queue and spend on one screen, with a drill-down into any run. It reads cox dash --feed, so it shows what the store shows. Its name through 0.34 was coxtop.

docs.title: What it owns
docs.text: The dash repository owns the towpath binary (Rust and ratatui), its themes and its keymap. Every action it offers is a cox verb; it holds no state of its own beyond the view you left it on.

docs.title: Installing it
docs.text:
Dash is optional: nothing else needs it. It lives in its own repository and is tagged on its own: a Coxswain release tags dash only when dash changed, and manifest.toml names the tag a release uses. Install it one of these ways.

With cox install. Pass --with dash.

Homebrew. The cox formula installs towpath along with cox:

brew install ppfenning/coxswain/cox

Release asset. Each dash release ships prebuilt binaries named towpath-<tag>-<target>.tar.gz. Download the one for your target from the release page of coxswain-dash and put towpath on your PATH.

Cargo, as the fallback. Build from source at the tag manifest.toml names (the crate is coxswain-dash; it installs towpath):

cargo install --git https://github.com/ppfenning/coxswain-dash --tag <dash tag>

docs.title: Its own docs
docs.text: The dash repository's own README lives at github.com/ppfenning/coxswain-dash.

docs.title: coxswain-dash
docs.text: towpath, the Coxswain fleet dashboard: a terminal view of the chair, spend, machines, lanes, runs, queue and inbox, built with ratatui. It reads cox dash --feed and runs every action as a cox command after a confirm that shows the command. Part of Coxswain.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: cox home opens towpath (bare cox starts a Claude session), so the towpath binary must be on your PATH.

docs.title: Homebrew
docs.text:
Installing cox from the tap installs towpath alongside it. No Rust toolchain is needed.

brew install <tap>/cox

docs.title: Release asset
docs.text:
Each release attaches a prebuilt archive for two platforms, each with a .sha256 sibling:

  • macOS arm64: towpath-<tag>-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz
  • Linux x86_64: towpath-<tag>-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz

No other platform has a prebuilt binary. Each archive holds both binaries, towpath and its alias, described below. Download the asset and its .sha256 file for your platform from the GitHub release page of this repository. Verify the checksum, extract, and move towpath to a directory on your PATH. This example is for macOS arm64.

shasum -a 256 -c towpath-<tag>-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz.sha256
tar -xzf towpath-<tag>-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz
mv towpath <a-directory-on-your-PATH>/

On Linux x86_64, use sha256sum -c in place of shasum -a 256 -c, and the x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu asset name.

docs.title: The coxtop alias
docs.text: coxtop was the previous name of this program. It remains as an alias that prints a one-line notice and then runs towpath. It goes away in 0.37. The crate is still named coxswain-dash.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
A development checkout keeps building from source with cargo build --release and needs Rust. This is the path for development only.

cargo run --bin towpath

Checks (the same three run in CI and in every build lane, from .agent-checks):

cargo fmt --check
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test

docs.title: Graphs
docs.text: A graph is the ordered set of nodes a run executes: plan, build, review, arbitrate, validate, and so on. It is defined once and reused by every run that needs that shape of work.

docs.title: What it owns
docs.text: The src/graphs folder holds the graphs, the harness that runs them (the gate, the budget, the checks, the records), and the runners that execute nodes. Eleven graphs register a subcommand: decompose, lifecycle, validate, review-diff and rescue-review for delivery, and cos, reconcile, retro, triage, triage-quarantine and sweep for operations. The epic driver, which runs an initiative phase by phase, is harness code, not a graph. See Graphs for the methodology behind the shape.

docs.title: Installing it
docs.text: Graphs ships in every install. The profile's harness_dir points at <checkout>/src/graphs, and the harness runs in the checkout's venv.

docs.title: Its own docs
docs.text: The folder's README and docs live at src/graphs.

docs.title: graphs
docs.text:
The graphs a run executes, and the harness that runs them. This folder is the harness, runner and graphs packages inside the coxswain repository; they ship as part of the one coxswain package. To install Coxswain, see the root README.

Four nouns, one seam each:

Noun Owns Lives in Harness consequences: side effects, policy, the gate, the ledger harness/ Graph sequence — what runs, in what order, at what tier. Writes nothing graphs/ Cartridge who a run works for: role → skill, where writes land ../cartridges Runner execution: canned dicts in tests, the model live runner/ 
harness/   the runtime. resolve, discover, run, gate, apply, record
graphs/    the programs. pure functions of (args, runner)
  delivery/   work that produces work: initiative-decompose, lifecycle-propose, phase-validate,
              review-diff, rescue-review
  ops/        keeping a running system honest: coxswain, epic-reconcile, retro-propose,
              triage-propose, triage, sweep
runner/    node execution: the protocol, a scripted runner, the live one
shell.py   the harness entry point: `python shell.py <graph> ...`
docs/      the contract every graph must satisfy, and one generated page per graph
fixtures/  canned runs and a small work store for offline runs and tests
tests/     this folder's suite, including the portability check

A graph is run(args, runner) -> dict. Nodes ask for a role and a tier, never a skill or a model: the cartridge maps role to skill, the provider profile maps tier to model. Nothing in a graph writes; the harness applies a proposal in a worktree it created, after the gate approved it. See docs/GRAPH-CONTRACT.md for the full contract.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
From this folder:

cd src/graphs && uv run pytest -q

The suite runs with no network and no key: ScriptedRunner replays canned nodes.

docs.title: Running one offline
docs.text:
From this folder, against the cartridges beside it:

scratch="$(mktemp -d)"
uv run python shell.py triage --team local \
  --cartridges-dir ../cartridges/cartridges \
  --skills-root ../cartridges/skills-plugins \
  --alerts fixtures/alerts.json \
  --scripted fixtures/triage-run.json --assume r \
  --runs-dir "$scratch" --ledger "$scratch/ledger.jsonl"

--scripted replays canned nodes, so no key is needed. --assume r (or a) answers the gate without asking. Pass --ledger as above for a throwaway run: without it the gate decisions are appended to the default ledger, $XDG_STATE_HOME/agent-graphs/ledger.jsonl, or ~/.local/state/agent-graphs/ledger.jsonl when XDG_STATE_HOME is unset. Drop --scripted to run against the real model; the provider profile decides which model each tier means. A host's cox route launch starts the harness the same way, with harness_dir set to <checkout>/src/graphs.

docs.title: The graphs
docs.text:
The registry is every module under graphs/ that declares a SPEC; harness/registry.py discovers them. shell.py takes the subcommand.

Graph Subcommand Namespace Shape initiative-decompose decompose delivery decompose → adversary-on-the-edges → emit. An idea into phases and a task DAG lifecycle-propose lifecycle delivery scope → plan → [alternative plan → arbitrate plans] → [attack the plan] → build (worktree) → handoff → review → adversary → arbitrate → emit phase-validate validate delivery validate_chunk per task → validate_phase against the phase's ORIGINAL goal. Invoked by the epic driver review-diff review-diff delivery review_charter → review_adversary → verify_evidence → [arbitrate]. Verdict and findings out, nothing written or pushed rescue-review rescue-review delivery handoff → review_charter → review_adversary → [arbitrate] → emit. A patch that already exists, reviewed with the harness's own check results coxswain cos ops one dispatch node over a driver-assembled docket. Selects; the harness invokes epic-reconcile reconcile ops compare (set arithmetic) → emit. Declared state vs actual retro-propose retro ops stats (pure arithmetic over ledger rows) → retro → emit. Proposes only what it can cite triage-propose triage ops fetch → classify → verify → emit. Zero writes; proposes corrections to the runbook it just used triage triage-quarantine ops facts (pure arithmetic over an item's attempts) → triage → emit. Classifies a stranded item at the attempt cap and emits by class, or escalates a repeated (class, diagnosis) pair sweep sweep ops sweep_plan → sweep_apply → sweep_verify → [review pair]. One rule applied everywhere it matches; sweep_apply calls a model only when the rule can't be scripted, one build call, and sweep_verify runs no model at all

shell.py also takes phase, epic and rescue. These are drivers, not graphs: they invoke graphs, block on them and own side effects, so they live in harness/ and declare no SPEC. epic is the epic driver (harness/epic.py, specified in graphs/delivery/epic-swarm.md), which cox route launch epic starts.

Each graph's diagram is generated from its own docstring by python -m harness.graphdoc; the committed pages live under docs/graphs/.

docs.text: MIT. See LICENSE.

docs.title: What a graph must satisfy
docs.text: A graph is an ordered set of agent nodes that reads a cartridge, does work, and emits proposals. It is the only layer that knows about sequence; it knows nothing about who it works for.

docs.title: Hard rules
docs.text:
1. Roles, never skills. A node declares the role it needs (plan, review_charter). The cartridge maps role → skill name. A graph that names a skill has bound itself to one team's plugin layout.

2. args.cartridge is required, with no fallback. Not "defaults to the last known config" — required, throw on absence. A fallback means the seam is never exercised, so it rots silently while the cartridge drifts, and the first symptom is a production run against year-old values.

3. No domain constants. Enforced, not requested — see tests/test_portability.py. Tracker IDs, hosts, buckets, ARNs, account numbers, usernames in paths: all read off the cartridge or absent.

4. Scripts have no filesystem access and cannot read the clock. Both are arguments. date is passed in for the same reason the cartridge is: a graph that reads the clock cannot be replayed, and a graph that cannot be replayed cannot be debugged after the fact.

5. Propose-only by default. Nodes are read-only. Proposals are data. The shell presents them at a gate and applies nothing without a decision. The one allowed exception is a build node writing into a worktree it owns — nothing pushed, nothing merged.

6. Caps are explicit and overflow is visible. Where a node bounds its work (structured-output limits are real), the overflow defers to the next run and is counted. Never silently truncate — a graph that drops nine of ten alerts and reports success on the tenth is worse than one that fails.

docs.title: Node shape
docs.text:
Each node declares: the role it fills, the capability tier it wants (cheap / standard / deep — resolved to a model by the provider profile), whether it is read-only, and what it returns.

Return shapes stay small. A node that hands the next node a large blob has moved the reasoning into the wrong place, and blows structured-output limits on a busy day.

docs.title: Proposal shape
docs.text:
{ kind, risk, target, evidence[], rationale, suggested_action }
  • kind must exist in the cartridge's write_kinds. Unknown kind → refuse.
  • evidence is deterministic checks and their output, not prose. A claim without evidence is not a proposal, it is a guess with formatting.
  • risk comes from the taxonomy, never invented at the node.

docs.title: The shell's duties, in order
docs.text:
Three, and the first one is easy to forget because the contract used only ever spelled out the last two:

1. Before the gate — measure, then escalate, then ask the policy. When --repo names the project a change targets, the harness applies the build patch in a real worktree of it and RUNS the cartridge's configured checks (landing_areas.checks) plus each command in the target repository's root .agent-checks file (one per line, added after the cartridge's), attaching pass/fail and parsed counts to the proposal the way change_facts already work — counted from reality, never asked of a model. Then, from the diff's paths alone, it escalates any patch-bearing proposal whose change touches governance (cartridges/, skills-plugins/, core/policy.py, core/ledger.py, harness/, the ledger file) to the self_modification kind, ramp: never, whatever kind the graph claimed — a system must not loosen its own rules on its own say-so. Only then: For every proposal, consult autonomy_policy against the ledger, filtered to this exact cartridge_sha and provider profile. Without this the gate asks about every kind forever, no streak is ever spent, and earned autonomy is decoration. This clause exists because the first implementation shipped policy.py fully unit-tested and never called it — a pure function cannot notice a caller that never calls it.

An auto-applied proposal gets no ledger row. The ledger records what happened at a gate, and an auto-apply never reached one. If acting on a streak could extend that streak, a kind would ratchet itself up forever on its own say-so, which is the self-report the ledger exists to disbelieve. Autonomy is spent by acting, re-earned only at the gate, and lost when a detector files an observation.

An apply arm is a role, so the same runner that ran the read-only nodes runs the write. An arm with no executor here (pr) goes to the gate rather than being reported as done.

2 and 3. After the run — two calls, not a ritual: build the manifest (which hashes the resolved cartridge), then record it — which derives ledger outcomes from the gate diffs rather than trusting anything the run says about itself.

docs.title: Review is proportional to cost, and nothing is one-shot
docs.text:
Every change gets a reviewer. How many it gets is decided by review_tier in the cartridge, not by the author:

Tier When Reviewers 0 matches tier0_patterns charter 1 within tier1_max_changed_lines / tier1_max_modules charter + adversary 2 touches a tier2_surfaces surface, or is simply big charter + adversary + arbitration, whether or not they disagreed

The dangerous-surface check runs first and cannot be talked down by size: a four-line migration outranks a four-hundred-line rename. Tier 0 is the cheapest review, never the absence of one. At tier 2, two reviewers agreeing is not by itself evidence — which is why arbitration runs anyway.

Reviewer roles are optional. A team that binds none of them gets a single reviewer, and an unbound adversary is not a silent objection.

docs.title: Steps hand off, and a handoff is checked
docs.text:
Between two steps sits a handoff node: does what the last step produced actually contain what the next one needs? If not, the graph stops. A reviewer handed half a change produces a confident opinion about the wrong thing, and a phase that goes quietly wrong usually did so several steps earlier.

Its second job is compression — the next step gets a small brief rather than everything that came before, which is the existing rule about return shapes staying small, enforced at the seam where it actually matters.

docs.title: The graphs
docs.text:
Graph Shape initiative-decompose decompose → adversary-on-the-edges → emit. Idea into phases and a task DAG. lifecycle-propose scope → plan → [alternative plan → arbitrate plans] → [attack the plan] → build (worktree) → handoff → review → adversary → arbitrate → emit. One task. triage facts (pure arithmetic over an item's attempts) → triage → emit. Classifies a stranded item at the attempt cap and emits by class, or escalates a repeated (class, diagnosis) pair. triage-propose fetch → classify → verify → emit. Zero writes; proposes its own runbook corrections. epic-reconcile compare (set arithmetic) → emit. Declared state vs actual. phase-validate validate_chunk per task → validate_phase against the phase's ORIGINAL goal. Invoked by the epic driver. retro-propose stats (pure arithmetic over ledger rows) → retro → emit. Proposes only what it can cite. sweep sweep_plan → sweep_apply → sweep_verify → [review pair]. Ceilings on sweep_plan and, only where a rule can't be scripted, the one sweep_apply build call; verify is a grep, no model. coxswain one dispatch node over a driver-assembled docket. Selects; the driver invokes. review-diff review_charter → review_adversary → verify_evidence → [arbitrate]. Reviews an arbitrary diff, outside any build's own run. rescue-review handoff → review_charter → review_adversary → [arbitrate] → emit. One review round over a patch that already exists.

All eleven are specified in graphs/, declare a SPEC, and are implemented. The table names each graph by its GRAPH_NAME; shell.py takes the subcommand its SPEC declares (for example decompose, lifecycle, validate, cos, reconcile, retro, and triage-quarantine for triage).

Running a phase is not a graph: the shell runs lifecycle-propose once per unblocked task, concurrently. Sequence belongs to a graph; concurrency belongs to the I/O edge that already owns every side effect. Results are ordered by task id before anything is recorded, so wall-clock order never reaches the ledger. The same ruling, made once in harness/invoke.py, governs everything that blocks on futures: the phase driver, the epic driver (harness/epic.py), and the coxswain driver (harness/cos.py). None of them carries a SPEC, and every child run records under the parent's run id.

docs.title: None of this needs a tracker
docs.text: The roles and write kinds name work, not vendors: work_state_arm, work_item_arm, item_create, state_move. The local cartridge (src/cartridges/cartridges/local/) binds every one of them to the filesystem — work items are markdown files under work/, git is the audit trail — and resolves with no tracker, no workspace id, and no auth_env. If a graph needed a tracker, that cartridge could not resolve.

docs.title: Trust is earned per runbook entry
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-09-01). src/cartridges/core/policy.py counts streaks per subject with a kind-level fallback and gates subject_new unconditionally; ledger rows carry the optional subject; triage's doc_update proposals name their entry; and the harness files a failure observation against an entry whose trap did not hold (harness/cli.py), so demotion no longer waits for a human to refuse something. The open questions below were resolved as: the incident signal enters as an argument-shaped observation from the harness after the run; blast radius is narrow (only the implicated entry); an amendment does not yet reset the entry's streak (deferred — it needs entry content hashing, and a wrong amendment still demotes on its next failure); the schema grew the nullable subject exactly as proposed; and the field was not generalised beyond graphs that have one.

docs.title: The gap
docs.text:
Today autonomy_policy measures a (kind, risk) pair, scoped to a cartridge_sha and a provider_profile. For triage that grain is too coarse in both directions.

doc_update is one kind. But a runbook index is not one thing — it is forty entries of wildly different quality. An entry that has classified the same symptom correctly thirty times and an entry written yesterday from a single sighting are, to the policy, indistinguishable: they graduate together, on a streak that is the average of every entry's behaviour. That average hides exactly the case worth catching. A kind can be riding a clean streak while one of its entries is quietly wrong every time it fires, because the other thirty-nine carry it.

And it fails the other way too. One bad entry poisons the streak for a kind that is otherwise trustworthy, so good entries are held back by a bad neighbour they have nothing to do with.

docs.title: The change
docs.text:
The runbook entry is the principal. Ledger rows from triage carry the entry they were produced under — rb-04 — and streaks are counted per entry, not just per kind. SCOPE_KEYS grows a third dimension for graphs that have one.

This does not contradict rule 6 ("the principal is the GRAPH, never a person"). It sharpens it. The thing being trusted was never really the category of write; it was the encoded judgment that produced it. In triage, that judgment lives in the runbook entry — its match, its checks, and its trap. Trusting doc_update in the abstract is trusting a container. Trusting rb-04 is trusting a claim that can actually be wrong.

docs.title: Incidents demote
docs.text:
An entry loses standing on any of three signals. The first already exists; the other two are new:

Signal Meaning Source Reversal a human edited or refused the proposal the gate, as today trap_held: false the entry's stated wrong belief was itself wrong verify already reports this An incident implicating the entry someone followed the runbook and it went wrong post-hoc, after the run

The second is the interesting one, because verify already reports it and today it only produces a doc_update proposal. An entry whose trap did not hold has been demonstrated to point at the wrong belief — that should reset its streak, not merely suggest an edit.

The third is the strongest reversal available and rule 3 already contemplates its shape ("a post-hoc detector fired"). An incident is the runbook being wrong in production, which is the only evidence that actually settles the question. It arrives late, after the row was written and possibly after the write auto-applied. That is fine: the ledger is append-only, and a later row demoting an entry is exactly how a track record should work.

docs.title: The asymmetry is the safety property
docs.text: An entry earns trust slowly — graduation_n consecutive clean outcomes — and loses it on a single incident, with regraduation_multiplier raising the bar it must clear to come back. Same shape as rule 3, applied at the grain where the judgment actually lives. Cheap to earn back a little, expensive to earn back after being wrong twice.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Where does the incident signal enter? Triage takes alerts as an argument precisely so the graph never reads a queue. An incident feed has the same constraint and probably the same answer: an argument, not a fetch.
  • Blast radius. Does an incident demote only the implicated entry, or its neighbours in the same symptom family? Narrow is more honest; wide is safer. Probably narrow, on the grounds that a policy that punishes uninvolved entries is one nobody will trust enough to leave switched on.
  • Does an amendment reset the streak? Likely yes — an amended entry is a new entry, and the track record belonged to the text that was replaced. This mirrors the cartridge-hash rule: a record earned under different rules is not a record.
  • Schema. Rows need a subject (nullable). Graphs without one behave exactly as today, so this is additive.
  • Generality. Triage has runbook entries; lifecycle-propose has none, or has something else. Worth resisting the urge to generalise the field before a second graph actually needs it.

docs.title: The project overlay layer
docs.text:
Status: implemented (2026-09-06). A fourth cartridge layer, read from the TARGET repository rather than from the cartridges folder itself: <repo>/.agent/cartridge.yaml. It has no extends — it is the last word, not another link in the chain — and it merges LAST, on top of whatever the profile's team cartridge already resolved to. Absent, the resolved cartridge is byte-identical to a run without one.

Only four top-level keys are read out of it:

  • context — concatenates onto the context list, as every layer does.
  • policy.review_tier — tighten only. An overlay may add a tier2 surface or lower a size threshold; it may not raise one or remove a surface the team already set.
  • policy.cost.level — tighten only: it may move toward strict, never toward liberal. Any other key under policy.cost is refused.
  • landing_areas.checks — the run's checks. An overlay's list REPLACES the team cartridge's list for that repository. The repository's root .agent-checks file is separate: its commands, one per line, are ADDED after the cartridge's (or overlay's) checks, skipping any cmd already listed. Each check entry takes name and cmd, and may take an optional timeout: an integer number of seconds greater than zero, applied to that one check only. When timeout is absent the check runs under the harness-wide default of 600 seconds. A value that is not an integer greater than zero is refused with ValueError.

landing_areas:
  checks:
    - name: pytest
      cmd: pytest -q
      timeout: 1200
- description.

Every other top-level key is refused. skills, cast, write_kinds, extends, and anything else the overlay declares raises CartridgeError naming the offending key — an overlay tightens a team's policy, it does not hand the target repository a second cast or a second set of write kinds.

The overlay's own text is folded into cartridge_sha, so a run under an overlay and a run without one are provably different runs. The resolved cartridge also carries overlay_sha: the sha256 of the overlay text when <repo>/.agent/cartridge.yaml was present, None when it was not.

The harness writes overlay_sha beside cartridge_sha wherever it builds a per-run record from the resolved cartridge: the entry-level observation _observe_trap_failures files when a doc_update trap did not hold (harness/cli.py), and the phase manifest, because build_manifest in src/cartridges/core/manifest.py reads overlay_sha off the cartridge it is handed.

docs.title: What a seat can see
docs.text: A build seat sees one repository worktree. It cannot analyse the platform's own operational record — the runs, ledgers, and usage accounting that the harness keeps about itself — because that record lives outside any single checkout and a ticket that asks a seat to reach for it is asking for something no seat can honestly answer. Those questions route instead to cox stats, which is the deterministic surface for roles, explain, coverage, and series; whatever it cannot answer, the chair answers by hand and files as a stats gap. A read-only analyst seat for this corpus is deferred, not built. The exact paths a ticket may not name are enforced by the reach rule and listed in docs/design/validator-reach.md §3, not repeated here.

docs.title: coxswain
docs.text:
One node, one role. Given a docket describing what is on hand right now — the graph registry, the intake queue, the ready set, the ledger's shape — decide which graphs to run next, and say why. That decision is judgment, exactly like every other decision this codebase hands to a model, so it lives in a graph like every other one: pure, replayable, no disk, no clock.

docs.title: epic-reconcile
docs.text:
lifecycle-propose scopes work into an epic. Nothing until now looked at whether the epic still describes reality afterwards, and epics drift: tickets get closed on the board and not in the epic, phases finish out of order, work gets added that nobody attached. An epic model that is only ever written and never checked degrades into a diagram of what someone once intended.

docs.title: phase-validate
docs.text:
The two validators the epic-swarm spec asks for, as a graph. They are model calls, and model calls belong in graphs — a driver that called the runner directly would be the first non-graph thing in the system to do so, and every purity rule the portability suite enforces would stop applying to the two nodes whose judgment the phase boundary rests on. So the driver invokes this the way it invokes any other graph, through invoke_graphs, and gets back an opinion rather than a decision.

docs.title: rescue-review
docs.text:
Takes a ticket, a patch and the evidence rows the harness produced by running the checks, and returns a verdict shaped like a lifecycle result so the driver reads it the same way. There is no plan node, no build node and no fix loop: one review round, and the verdict is final.

docs.title: retro-propose
docs.text:
A retro over a running system is not a model asked "how did we do" from memory — memory is exactly what the ledger exists to disbelieve. So the stats this graph reasons about are computed HERE, mechanically, as pure dict arithmetic over the rows the harness read: per (kind, subject) bucket, the outcome counts, the current consecutive-clean streak (a clean that took more than one build attempt is transparent, same rule the policy itself uses so a struggling loop cannot manufacture the record it stands on), the reversal count, and how many cleans were not first-try.

    n1["retro<br/>step · 2"]
    n2["emit<br/>step · 3"]
    n0 --> n1
    n1 --> n2
    style n0 fill:#f96,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px

Takes a diff, a repo and a ref — never a run's own build branch — and returns the same verdict-and-findings shape a build's own review step produces. Nothing is written to the repo and nothing is pushed.

docs.title: sweep
docs.text:
The complement to decompose: work that needs no per-unit design, only one judgment call applied everywhere it matches. sweep_plan reads the whole repository through its own tool loop and writes the map, the exceptions and the application; this module never touches a filesystem itself outside sweep_apply, which is the edge that runs the script or the one build call. sweep_verify takes what sweep_apply already captured — no model, no I/O of its own — and the review pair on the one resulting diff is review-diff, the same pair every other graph here uses, not a copy of it.

docs.text:
Alerts arrive as an argument rather than being fetched here. A graph that reads a queue reads the world, and the contract puts both the filesystem and the clock on the far side of the graph boundary for the same reason: a graph that cannot be replayed cannot be debugged after the fact.

docs.title: triage
docs.text:
The triage role classifies a stranded item against facts and must cite the record; emit builds the write by class — a ticket_amend proposal, an item_create proposal, a decompose handoff, or a notify proposal — and refuses to repeat an already-fired (class, diagnosis) pair on the same item, escalating to a person instead.
