docs.title: Start it
docs.text:
You need Docker with the compose plugin. From the repository root:

cd deploy/superset
cp .env.example .env

Open .env and replace every placeholder.

  • SUPERSET_SECRET_KEY signs sessions. Generate a value with openssl rand -base64 42.
  • SUPERSET_ADMIN_PASSWORD is the password for the admin user. Keep the other admin values or change them.
  • COXSWAIN_S3_ENDPOINT is the S3-compatible endpoint of the Garage-backed Iceberg lake. Empty skips the lake entirely.
  • COXSWAIN_S3_KEY_ID is the access key id for that endpoint.
  • COXSWAIN_S3_SECRET is the secret access key for that endpoint.
  • COXSWAIN_S3_REGION is the region DuckDB sends with each S3 request. Garage accepts any string; it defaults to garage when left empty.

SUPERSET_SECRET_KEY and every admin variable must be set, and compose refuses to start when one is empty or still reads change-me. COXSWAIN_STORE_URL and the COXSWAIN_S3_* variables carry no such check: they default to empty, and an empty COXSWAIN_S3_ENDPOINT just skips the lake. Never commit .env.

docker compose up -d

The first start builds the image, so it takes a while. Then open http://127.0.0.1:8088. The port is bound to your machine only.

docs.title: Log in and open the dashboard
docs.text:
Log in with SUPERSET_ADMIN_USERNAME and SUPERSET_ADMIN_PASSWORD from your .env. The username is admin unless you changed it.

Open the Dashboards list from the top menu and choose the Coxswain dashboard.

docker compose up -d also runs the superset-dashboards one-shot service once Superset is healthy, and that service installs the dashboards. It reads the specs in deploy/superset/dashboards and skips each dataset, with its charts, until the source it requires answers a readiness probe. Run it again after a spec changes, or once the store or the lake first answers. A second run changes nothing when the specs already match Superset.

Readiness comes from a probe, not a file check. Before installing anything, bootstrap runs one SELECT ... WHERE false per required table through SQL Lab, never LIMIT 0; a WHERE false select fails on a missing table or column exactly like a real query would, and reads no row when it succeeds. A SQL Lab answer whose JSON body carries an errors key counts as absent, whatever HTTP status it arrived on: 200, 400, 422 and 500 all read the same way. A 401 or 403, or a network error the HTTP call itself raises, is not treated as absent; it propagates and stops bootstrap instead of quietly skipping a dataset.

docker compose run --rm superset-dashboards

To confirm every chart returns data, export the values from your .env and run the check from the repository root. It prints one line per chart, <chart>: <rows> rows or <chart>: ERROR <message>, and exits 1 if any chart errors.

python deploy/superset/check.py

docs.title: Fleet
docs.text:
The Fleet dashboard answers five questions about the machines running Coxswain, one chart per panel.

  • Chair holder, epoch and beat age. Who holds the chair lease, which host and epoch it holds it at, and how many seconds have passed since its last heartbeat.
  • Lanes per host over time against capacity. How many lanes each host ran per hour over the last 14 days, next to the max-in-flight limit in force at that hour.
  • Host state and last login. Every host's state and when it last checked in.
  • Needs-chair items by cause. How many tasks are waiting on the chair, grouped by why, and how long the oldest one in each group has waited.
  • Weekly spend against the ceiling. Cumulative spend since the most recent weekly reset, next to the weekly_fraction the chair loop recorded at each point.

There is no drafts panel yet. The store keeps no draft or approval state on task_records, so a dataset that lists items waiting on a draft has no column to filter on; see the fleet_drafts_waiting_approval comment in deploy/superset/dashboards/datasets.yaml.

Fleet reads the store only: chair_actions, hosts, leases, runs, and node_calls. An earlier ticks table that used to sit alongside chair_actions is gone from this list; nothing ever wrote to it, so no Fleet dataset reads it. Fleet reads these tables through the same connection as the Coxswain and Chair dashboards, sqlite_scan of cox.db or an attached Postgres catalog, and never chair.actions.jsonl, land.jsonl, or any other log file. None of its datasets reads task_records.

The host-state panel is skipped until the hosts table is readable. fleet_host_state requires store, the same single requirement every Fleet dataset carries, and bootstrap installs a dataset only once its required source answers its probe. Once a run has written to hosts, rerun docker compose run --rm superset-dashboards to install the panel.

bootstrap.py creates every Fleet chart from the specs in deploy/superset/dashboards/charts.yaml, but it still groups only the Coxswain charts into a Superset dashboard page. The comment atop deploy/superset/dashboards/dashboard.yaml names teaching it to also build the Fleet and Chair pages as a separate, later change. Until then, open Charts from the top menu and find a panel by its title; a chart opened this way shows the same query a dashboard page would.

Four of the five panels read a dataset new to Fleet. Their SQL, copied from deploy/superset/dashboards/datasets.yaml:

chair_lanes_by_host_hour feeds Lanes per host over time against capacity:

WITH hours AS (
  SELECT h AS hour_start, h + INTERVAL 1 HOUR AS hour_end
  FROM generate_series(
    date_trunc('hour', CAST(now() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AS TIMESTAMP)) - INTERVAL 14 DAY,
    date_trunc('hour', CAST(now() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AS TIMESTAMP)),
    INTERVAL 1 HOUR
  ) AS t(h)
),
r AS (
  SELECT CAST(launched_at AS TIMESTAMP) AS launched_at, CAST(ended_at AS TIMESTAMP) AS ended_at,
         COALESCE(NULLIF(host, ''), 'local') AS host
  FROM {{store:runs}}
),
busy AS (
  SELECT hours.hour_start, r.host, COUNT(*) AS lanes
  FROM hours
  JOIN r ON r.launched_at <= hours.hour_end
        AND COALESCE(r.ended_at, CAST(now() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AS TIMESTAMP)) >= hours.hour_start
  GROUP BY ALL
)
SELECT busy.hour_start AS hour, busy.host, busy.lanes, hosts.capacity
FROM busy
LEFT JOIN {{store:hosts}} AS hosts ON hosts.name = busy.host
ORDER BY hour, host

fleet_host_state feeds Host state and last login:

SELECT name, state, capacity, CAST(beat_at AS TIMESTAMP) AS beat_at,
       CAST(json_extract(versions_json, '$.login_ok') AS BOOLEAN) AS login_ok,
       CAST(json_extract_string(versions_json, '$.login_checked_at') AS TIMESTAMP) AS login_checked_at
FROM {{store:hosts}}

fleet_needs_chair_by_cause feeds Needs-chair items by cause:

WITH flagged AS (
  SELECT target, json_extract_string(action_json, '$.reason') AS reason, CAST(ts AS TIMESTAMP) AS flagged_at,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY target ORDER BY CAST(ts AS TIMESTAMP) DESC) AS rn
  FROM {{store:chair_actions}} WHERE kind = 'needs_chair'
),
landed AS (
  SELECT target, CAST(ts AS TIMESTAMP) AS landed_at
  FROM {{store:chair_actions}} WHERE kind IN ('land', 'land_phase') AND status = 'landed'
),
waiting AS (
  SELECT f.reason, f.flagged_at
  FROM flagged AS f
  WHERE f.rn = 1
    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM landed AS l WHERE l.target = f.target AND l.landed_at > f.flagged_at
    )
)
SELECT reason AS cause, COUNT(*) AS items,
       MAX(date_diff('minute', flagged_at, CAST(now() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AS TIMESTAMP))) / 60.0 AS oldest_waiting_hours
FROM waiting
GROUP BY reason

fleet_weekly_spend feeds Weekly spend against the ceiling:

SELECT date_trunc('week', CAST(ts AS TIMESTAMP)) AS week, SUM(cost_usd) AS cost_usd
FROM {{store:node_calls}}
WHERE CAST(ts AS TIMESTAMP) >= date_trunc('week', CAST(now() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AS TIMESTAMP)) - INTERVAL 12 WEEK
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1

The fifth panel, Chair holder, epoch and beat age, reads the chair_status dataset.

docs.title: Chair
docs.text:
The Chair dashboard answers three questions about the always-on chair loop, one chart per panel.

  • Chair actions per hour by kind. How many actions the loop took each hour, split by kind: land, launch_epic, launch_decompose, rescue, relaunch, needs_chair, or standby. It reads the chair_actions_by_hour dataset.
  • Spend per landed task per day. The day's model spend divided by the tasks the loop landed that day, next to the loop's own cost per landed task. It reads the chair_spend_by_day dataset.
  • Needs-chair backlog. Which tasks are waiting on the chair right now, and how long the oldest one has waited. It reads the chair_needs_backlog dataset.

The loop makes no model calls itself, so its line in the spend panel is zero by construction. It exists for contrast with the interactive chair, which does call a model, so the two lines show a loop that costs nothing next to one that does.

Chair reads the store only: chair_actions and node_calls. The same ticks table Fleet no longer lists is gone from here too; nothing ever wrote to it, so no Chair dataset reads it. Chair reads these tables through the same connection as the Coxswain and Fleet dashboards, and never chair.actions.jsonl, land.jsonl, or any other log file. None of its datasets reads task_records; a task counts as landed from its chair_actions row, as the comment above the chair datasets in datasets.yaml explains.

Like Fleet, bootstrap.py creates each Chair chart but still groups only the Coxswain charts into a dashboard page. Open Charts from the top menu and find a panel by its title.

docs.title: Crew
docs.text:
The Crew dashboard has eleven charts. They fall into five groups: cost and turns, approval and attempts, verdicts, quarantines, and efficiency. Crew reads the store only, through the crew_calls, crew_quarantines, crew_tasks, crew_reviews and crew_task_roles datasets.

Cost and turns:

  • Crew cost per day by role. How much each role spent each day.
  • Crew cost per day by model. How much each model alias spent each day.
  • Crew turns per day by role. How many turns each role took each day.

Approval and attempts:

  • First-try approval rate by builder seat. What share of each builder seat's tasks were approved on the first build attempt.
  • Build attempts per approved task by builder seat. How many build attempts each builder seat needed on the tasks that were approved.

Verdicts:

  • Crew reviewer verdict mix. How the charter reviewer's verdicts split across the adversary's verdicts.
  • Arbiter sides with the adversary. Which side the arbiter took on the tasks it ruled on.

Quarantines:

  • Quarantines by role and cause, last 14 days. Which roles had attempts quarantined, and why.
  • Quarantines by repository and cause, last 14 days. Which repositories had attempts quarantined, and why.

Efficiency:

  • Cache-read share by role. What share of each role's input tokens came from the cache over the last two weeks.
  • Cost per approved task per role. What each role spends for every approved task.

Some terms are easy to misread. A task is first-try when it is approved with exactly one build attempt. The builder seat is the model alias of the task's build calls, taken from the earliest build call. A quarantine is an attempt of kind refused, unverified, infra or dropped, and an attempt with no cause is counted as unclassified. The arbiter chart leaves out tasks with no arbitration, so it counts only tasks the arbiter ruled on. Cost per approved task divides a role's cost on approved tasks by the number of approved tasks.

The datasets state fallbacks that the charts inherit. No approved marker has been found in the store, so a task counts as approved when its final review verdict is approve. That verdict is the arbiter's when the arbiter ruled and the reviewer's otherwise. It does not read the landed state, so an approved task that has not landed yet counts as approved. A quarantined attempt takes its role from the last model call for the same run and task. It takes its repository from runs.repo, joined on the run. An attempt with no matching call or run keeps its row with an empty role or repository. The datasets mark as unknown whether runs.repo exists, and that approve is the stored verdict string.

docs.title: The lake
docs.text:
The lake carries six tables: runs, phases, node_calls, gate_decisions, ledger, and traces. Only node_calls, runs and traces back a dataset today.

calls and calls_by_day read {{lake:node_calls}}. runs and lanes_by_hour read {{lake:runs}}. traces reads {{lake:traces}}. daily_efficiency and task_outcomes read {{lake:node_calls}}, and landed_tasks reads {{lake:node_calls}} and {{lake:runs}}; all three also read the store's task_records table, through {{store:task_records}} (see Efficiency).

Every Fleet and Chair dataset reads the store only, through {{store:<table>}}, and requires store rather than lake. Two more datasets, attempts and task_verdicts, read the store only too but still carry requires: lake in datasets.yaml, so bootstrap skips them until the lake probe succeeds even though their SQL never touches it.

The traces dataset now reads {{lake:traces}} instead of scanning local Parquet files, so a trace that graphs has pruned from disk still shows up in the tool-use chart; the lake keeps its history after the local file is gone.

A dataset with requires: lake is skipped, with its charts, until the lake probe succeeds, the same way a requires: store dataset waits on the store probes.

docs.title: Verify Fleet and Chair
docs.text:
Bring the stack up and install the specs, from deploy/superset:

docker compose up -d
docker compose run --rm superset-dashboards

Then export the values from your .env and run the check from the repository root.

python deploy/superset/check.py

It prints one line per chart, <chart>: <rows> rows or <chart>: ERROR <message>, and exits 1 if any chart errors. Among its lines are the five Fleet charts and the three Chair charts: Chair holder, epoch and beat age; Lanes per host over time against capacity; Host state and last login; Needs-chair items by cause; Weekly spend against the ceiling; Chair actions per hour by kind; Spend per landed task per day; Needs-chair backlog. A clean run exits 0.

Open each chart from the Charts list at http://127.0.0.1:8088 to see it rendered.

  • Chair holder, epoch and beat age is healthy when it shows one row with a holder, host and epoch, and a beat age of a few seconds, well under the chair's heartbeat interval.
  • Lanes per host over time against capacity is healthy when each host's line sits at or below its max-in-flight line.
  • Host state and last login is healthy when every host reads a known state with a recent last login check.
  • Needs-chair items by cause is healthy when it is empty, or short; a large oldest-waiting-hours value means the chair loop is behind.
  • Weekly spend against the ceiling is healthy when the cumulative line rises but stays under the ceiling for the week.
  • Chair actions per hour by kind is healthy when it shows a bar for most hours, mostly land and standby.
  • Spend per landed task per day is healthy when the loop's line sits flat at zero next to the interactive chair's nonzero line.
  • Needs-chair backlog is healthy when it is empty; a growing table means tasks are waiting longer than the loop is clearing them.

docs.title: Change the time range
docs.text: The dashboard has a time range filter. Open it, pick a range such as the last week or a pair of dates, and apply it. Every chart on the dashboard redraws for that range.

docs.title: Add a chart
docs.text:
Charts are built from a dataset, which is a saved SQL query or table.

  1. Open SQL Lab from the top menu.
  2. Choose the Coxswain database and write a query. Run it and check the rows.
  3. Choose Save as chart. Superset saves the query as a dataset and opens the chart editor.
  4. Pick a chart type, set its columns, and save the chart.
  5. Add the chart to a dashboard from the save dialog.

docs.title: The data is read-only
docs.text:
There is no COXSWAIN_RUNS_DIR and no /data/runs mount any more. No service in docker-compose.yml mounts a runs directory; the store and the lake are read over the network instead. The store connection attaches Postgres with READ_ONLY (attach_sql in superset_config.py); the lake connection only creates DuckDB views over iceberg_scan (lake_view_sql), which has no write path. Superset can query both but cannot change them.

With COXSWAIN_STORE_URL and COXSWAIN_S3_ENDPOINT set, every dataset runs on any machine that reaches the store and Garage: that includes daily_efficiency, landed_tasks and task_outcomes, which read landed rows from the store's task_records table, not from a local file. Queries read the store and the lake each time they run, so a refresh shows new data with no import step.

Superset keeps its own users, datasets, and charts in a separate Docker volume. Removing that volume loses your charts and never touches the store or the lake.

docs.title: Point the dashboard at Postgres
docs.text:
Set COXSWAIN_STORE_URL in .env to your Postgres store's URL. The URL below is a placeholder.

COXSWAIN_STORE_URL=postgresql://reader:change-me@db.example:5432/coxswain

Use a read-only Postgres role. The connection is attached read-only, but the role is the real limit. The store's tables must sit in the public schema of the database the URL names. A table in another schema fails when a chart queries it.

With the variable set, the datasets read the store through an attached catalog named store. Their SQL reads store.public.<table>. With it unset or empty, dataset SQL still falls back to a sqlite_scan of /data/runs/cox.db, but nothing mounts that path any more, so the store probes fail and bootstrap skips every store dataset, with its charts. In practice the deploy needs COXSWAIN_STORE_URL set.

The superset-dashboards one-shot writes that SQL into the datasets. docker compose up -d runs it, as described above. If it did not run, the datasets keep their old SQL. Run it by hand after changing the variable.

docker compose run --rm superset-dashboards

Readiness in Postgres mode comes from the same probes as any other mode. Bootstrap runs the chair, hosts and lake probes through SQL Lab on the database Superset already has; it never checks for a local file. Until those probes succeed it skips the datasets that need them, with their charts, the same way it does on the first run against a new server.

The attached catalog was chosen over postgres_scan. A postgres_scan call takes the connection string in its arguments. That puts the password in the SQL of every dataset, and Superset saves that SQL. An attached catalog is set up by the connection, not by the query. The dataset SQL names a table in the catalog and never holds a URL.

A connect hook in superset_config.py does the attaching. Each time Superset opens a DuckDB connection, the hook reads COXSWAIN_STORE_URL from the container environment and runs ATTACH with it. So the password lives only in that environment. The saved database object and the dataset SQL hold no URL.

The same hook loads the lake, and only after that ATTACH. With COXSWAIN_STORE_URL unset it returns before the lake step, whatever the COXSWAIN_S3_* variables hold; the lake's table list is also read from the attached store, from store.public.iceberg_tables. Set COXSWAIN_STORE_URL and COXSWAIN_S3_ENDPOINT together to read the lake. The "Shared storage" section of Several machines puts traces and the lake on Garage, through traces_url, lake_url and an object_store block in the provider profile.

docs.title: Other data sources
docs.text:
The Superset image queries with DuckDB, so a dataset can read any source DuckDB reads.

A Postgres store. See the section above, which sets it up without putting the password in any SQL.

Traces. Traces come from the lake now, through {{lake:traces}}; see The lake. No dataset needs a shared Parquet location any more.

A local file. No container mounts a host directory. A dataset that must read one needs a volume added to docker-compose.yml first, which is a change to the deploy files and ties the deploy to the machine that holds the file.

docs.title: Efficiency
docs.text: This page shows where Coxswain's cost and speed numbers come from and which views read them. Each view answers one question about whether the system is getting cheaper and faster.

docs.title: Where the numbers come from
docs.text: Every model call is a row in the run store. The row carries its cost, its turns, its tokens, and its task.

docs.title: The dashboard
docs.text:
The Efficiency section of the Coxswain dashboard charts these questions. See Dashboards to run it.

  • Cost per turn by model.
  • Cache-read share.
  • Cost per landed task.
  • Landed per day.
  • First-try build rate.
  • Lead time.
  • Spend by task outcome.

Quarantines by cause is also a chart.

docs.title: cox stats gates
docs.text: For each review step, cox stats gates shows its cost and how often its verdict changed the outcome. It flags steps that change fewer than 5% of outcomes. Those steps are candidates for a cheaper tier, or for skipping on small tasks.

docs.title: cox stats tiers
docs.text:
For each role and model, cox stats tiers shows the landed rate, the first-try rate, and the cost per landed task.

It picks the cheapest model within 5 points of the best landed rate. Each model needs at least 20 tasks to count. It then shows what the pick would have saved.

The command changes nothing. To apply a pick, edit your provider profile.

docs.title: cox stats causes
docs.text: cox stats causes groups quarantined attempts by cause, with sample reasons. The causes are ticket, code, review, harness, and unknown.

docs.title: The docket
docs.text: cox route context prints an efficiency line for today.

docs.title: Fragments
docs.text: This page settles what a fragment is, where it lives, and the rule that governs one: cartridge.d/*.yaml, folded in sorted order, checked against everything folded before it.

docs.title: cartridge.d/*.yaml
docs.text:
A fragment is a small YAML file that adds to one cartridge layer. It has the same keys as cartridge.yaml. Fragments for a layer live beside that layer's cartridge.yaml, in cartridge.d/, one concern per file:

cartridges/my-team/
  cartridge.yaml
  cartridge.d/
    10-review.yaml
    20-checks.yaml
  context/
    charter.md

Prose (a charter, conventions) does not go in a fragment. It goes in a markdown file that a context: list names. A fragment can add to that list; its paths resolve from the team directory, not from cartridge.d/.

docs.title: Sorted order
docs.text:
Each layer folds its fragments in the sorted order of their file names, after the layer's own cartridge.yaml. Base's fragments fold before base joins local, and a team's fragments fold last. A later value wins a scalar conflict, so the file name is part of the contract. Number the files when order matters.

A fragment's extends key is ignored: the chain is fixed by each layer's cartridge.yaml before any fragment is read. An empty fragment folds as nothing.

docs.title: Tighten-only
docs.text: Each fragment is checked against the accumulated authority at its point: the parent chain, the layer's cartridge.yaml, and every fragment folded before it. A fragment that lowers a write kind's risk or shortens its ramp is refused, and the refusal names the fragment file. This is the rule in Cartridges, applied one file at a time.

docs.title: Changing a fragment
docs.text:
Edit the file and commit it in your workspace's cartridges folder. Every fragment's content is part of cartridge_sha, so changing one resets the autonomy streaks the old rules earned. To see the result, resolve the cartridge:

cartridge --team my-team --cartridges-dir <workspace>/cartridges --json

docs.title: The lake
docs.text: This page shows how to sync your Coxswain runs into an Iceberg lake, keep it fresh, and query it with SQL. It assumes you have never used Iceberg.

docs.title: Install it
docs.text:
The lake needs extra packages. Add the lake extra to cox, which is installed editable from the coxswain checkout:

uv tool install --force --editable "$HOME/.local/share/coxswain/installs/coxswain[lake]"

The install replaces the extras cox had, so name each one you use, such as [postgres,lake].

cox upgrade keeps the extras cox was installed with.

The extra brings pyiceberg with a SQL catalog, and duckdb.

docs.title: Sync your runs
docs.text:
cox lake sync appends the rows of each ended run to Iceberg tables. The tables are runs, phases, node_calls, gate_decisions, ledger, and traces.

  • Once. Each table has its own mark, so a run is appended once.
  • In place. The Parquet trace files are registered where they sit. Nothing is copied.
  • Dry run. --dry-run writes nothing.
  • Housekeeping. The chair loop's housekeeping runs cox lake sync and a trace prune, both at the same log_retention_days age.

docs.title: Archive your logs
docs.text:
Each ended run also leaves a <run>.log and a <run>.calls.jsonl. cox lake sync archives the ones older than log_retention_days days, a routing-profile key that defaults to 7; a missing, invalid, or non-positive value falls back to 7 too.

  • Where they go. Archived logs land at logs/<yyyy>/<mm>/<file>.gz, beside the traces root: a traces root ending in /traces becomes /logs, so s3://coxswain/traces becomes s3://coxswain/logs. The year and month come from the file's last write, in UTC.
  • Verified before deleted. The local file is deleted only after the archived copy reads back identical. A failed archive keeps the local file and is reported.
  • Reporting. cox lake sync prints a logs line only when some logs were due. --dry-run reports what would be synced and writes nothing; --json prints the report as JSON.
  • Kept indefinitely. The lake tables (runs, phases, node_calls, gate_decisions, ledger, traces) and the archived logs are kept indefinitely.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
Two values in your provider profile say where the lake is.

  • lake_url. The warehouse, e.g. s3://coxswain/lake.
  • lake_catalog_url. The Iceberg catalog. Any SQLAlchemy URL works, e.g. postgresql+psycopg://user@host:5432/db, which lets every machine that reaches the database find the tables.

With neither set, both default to files under the runs directory: lake-catalog.db and lake/.

docs.title: Query it
docs.text: cox lake query "<sql>" runs read-only DuckDB SQL over the lake tables. Add --json to get the result as JSON.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text: cox lake doctor checks the object store, the catalog, the namespace, the warehouse, and each table, and exits 1 on a failed check. It creates nothing.

docs.title: Keep it fresh
docs.text: After the first sync, cox runs land syncs after each land.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text: Coxswain's core repository names no vendor. Anything that talks to a particular tracker, forge, model vendor or hosted service is a plugin: a Python package that registers under an entry-point group, which core looks up by name. The public coxswain-plugins repository holds the ones Coxswain ships.

docs.title: The groups
docs.text:
Group Loaded by Chosen by Built in coxswain.sources cox route pull --source <name>, configured under the profile's sources.<name>; a bare pull reads every configured source github (issues labelled intake and PRs labelled review, through gh) and folder coxswain.forges cox runs land the profile's forge: key local (plain git, the default), github, forgejo, and auto (each repository's forge, from its origin) coxswain.trackers cox route sync the profile's tracker: key none (the default) and github-projects coxswain.system_one the harness's fast path the provider profile's system_one.backend model-tier coxswain.runners the harness the provider profile's runner: key claude-code and anthropic coxswain.storage the harness's trace store the URL's scheme file and s3 (built in)

A name that is neither built in nor registered is refused with a line naming the group, except in system one: an unregistered backend turns system one off for that run, and the run goes on without it.

docs.title: Built-in sources
docs.text:
Both run locally: github through your own gh login, folder on the filesystem. Name them in the routing profile, and map each listed repo or folder to the repository its tickets target:

sources: {"github": {"repos": ["owner/repo"]}, "folder": {"repos": ["~/intake"]}}
repo_map: {"owner/repo": "/path/to/repo", "~/intake": "/path/to/repo"}
  • github files each issue labelled intake (filter: label:<name> picks another label), then swaps the label for intake:taken and comments the intake path. An open PR labelled review is reviewed instead, and relabelled review:taken.
  • folder files each *.md directly in the folder: its first # heading is the title (else the file name), the rest the body. A filed file moves into the folder's done/, so the folder holds only what is waiting. The same name with new text files again.

The autonomous chair runs a bare cox route pull when it has free lanes and nothing else queued, so it reads every configured source.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
cox loads sources, forges and trackers from its own environment. cox is installed editable from the coxswain checkout, so add the plugins to that install:

uv tool install --force --editable ~/.local/share/coxswain/installs/coxswain \
  --with "coxswain-plugins @ git+https://github.com/ppfenning/coxswain-plugins"

The harness loads system-one backends and runners from the checkout's venv:

uv pip install --python ~/.local/share/coxswain/installs/coxswain/.venv/bin/python \
  "coxswain-plugins[jev] @ git+https://github.com/ppfenning/coxswain-plugins"

cox upgrade reinstalls cox with only the extras it had, which drops the --with package, so run the first command again after an upgrade. Its venv sync keeps packages the lock does not name, so the second survives.

A plugin that needs a vendor's client library declares it as an extra, as jev does. Installing one plugin never pulls in another's dependencies. cox setup doctor lists what each side can load in its plugins row.

docs.title: Writing one
docs.text:
Register the entry point in your package's pyproject.toml:

[project.entry-points."coxswain.forges"]
myforge = "my_package.forge"

Each group expects a different shape:

  • Source (a module): candidates(config, listing) -> tuple[Ref, ...], read(raw) -> Candidate, taken(link, intake_links) -> bool and mark_argv(ref, intake_path) -> list[str]. The profile's sources.<name> block gives repos, filter and token_env. An adapter reads a tracker and files intake tickets. It never moves the tracker's state.
  • Forge (a module): find_open_prs(repo, branch), push(repo, branch), open_pr(repo, title, body, *, head=None, base=None), wait_checks(repo, timeout_s, *, ref="HEAD") and merge(repo, step). Each except the first returns (ok, detail). merge updates the local default branch without checking anything out.
  • Tracker (a module): sync(workspace, items, *, dry_run) -> (ok, lines). cox route sync reads the work store's items, applies --item if given, and hands them over. items are the work store's initiatives and tasks: each has an id, title, body, repo, state, phase, run, cost, gate, issue and parent. Return ok and the lines to print, and write nothing when dry_run is true. An exception is reported as the tracker failing, and route sync exits 1.
  • System-one backend (a callable): make(model, api_key, block) returns a decider whose decide(question, state) returns an answer with a confidence. Set make.needs_key = True for a hosted service. Its key then comes only from the environment variable named in system_one.key_env, never from the provider's own key. Set make.wants_runner = True to be handed the run's runner as runner=. A backend runs in shadow until cox stats system-one says it has graduated.
  • Runner (a callable): factory(profile, *, role_skills, workdir, repo) returns a runner whose run(*, role, tier, schema, prompt, ...) returns the node's structured result.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text: This page settles what each policy knob changes and what a sane default looks like, for the values most teams touch first. Every key here lives under policy: in a cartridge. The values quoted are base's.

docs.title: review_tier
docs.text:
How much review a change must survive. The harness puts each change in one of three tiers:

Tier Who reviews 0 The charter reviewer alone. 1 The charter reviewer and the adversary. 2 Both, and the arbiter runs whether or not they disagree.

The keys decide the tier:

  • tier2_surfaces (base: schema, migration, deletion, auth, infrastructure, cross_repo, production_write_path). A change on any of these is tier 2, whatever its size. This check runs first.
  • tier0_patterns (base: docs_only, rename_only, config_bump, param_tweak). A change whose patterns are all in this list is tier 0.
  • tier0_max_changed_lines (base: 30). A change this small, in one module, is tier 0. Unset or 0 turns this off.
  • tier1_max_changed_lines (base: 150) and tier1_max_modules (base: 1). A change within both is tier 1. Anything bigger is tier 2.

No tier skips review. Tier 0 is the cheapest review, not none.

docs.title: plan_competition.min_tier
docs.text: The pre-build tier at which the plan competition runs: a second, independent plan, an arbiter that picks or merges the two, and an attacker that tests the chosen plan before anyone builds it. The tier is judged from the task's surfaces and patterns, since no diff exists yet. Base sets 1. Set 0 to run the competition on every task, or 3 to never run it.

docs.title: build_budget_usd_max
docs.text: The most a work item may ask for with its own budget_usd: field. Base sets 6.0, the runaway ceiling. A build without budget_usd uses its measured guide. The harness refuses an item that asks for more than this and quotes the number. See Budgets.

docs.title: dispatch.max_in_flight
docs.text: How many harness runs the chair may have alive at once on one machine. Base sets 3. It applies per machine; each lane host has its own capacity in the hosts table. A sane default is small enough that a person reviewing pull requests is not handed more at once than they can read.

docs.title: gate
docs.text: How far a land goes without a person: ticket (base), phase, epic or full. See Landing.

docs.title: pacing
docs.text:
How a launch reasons about the 5-hour window: window_hours, spent_vs_elapsed_margin, late_threshold, min_headroom_usd, and the tier_ladder and effort_ladder a launch degrades along.

The hard stops are not cartridge keys. The chair reads hard_stop_fraction (default 0.99) and weekly_hard_stop_fraction (default 0.93) from <runs>/policy.pacing.json in the workspace. See Autonomous chair.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text: This page settles what a provider profile controls: which tier a seat runs on, how much effort it spends, its dollar ceiling, and which tools it's allowed to call, per role.

docs.title: What a profile sets, per role
docs.text:
A provider profile is not one setting for the whole run. For each role — builder, charter reviewer, adversary, arbiter, validator — the profile sets:

  • tier — which model tier fills that role.
  • effort — how much of that tier's budget the role is expected to spend.
  • ceilings — the dollar limit the role can't exceed before the node stops (see Budgets for what happens then).
  • tools — which tools that role is allowed to call at all.

Two roles on the same run can run on different tiers with different tool lists; an adversary doesn't need the same tools a builder does, and running it on a cheaper tier is a profile decision, not a code change.

docs.title: Which providers exist
docs.text:
manifest.toml names which providers are available and which are ready to use:

claude-code = { status = "supported", profile = "providers/claude-code.yaml" }
codex       = { status = "planned" }
gemini      = { status = "planned" }
local       = { status = "experimental", profile = "providers/local-oss.yaml" }

Only claude-code is status = "supported" today. local is status = "experimental": its profile, providers/local-oss.yaml, declares its capabilities and puts the cheap tier on a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint, but no runner drives it yet. The others are status = "planned" and have no profile to point at.

docs.title: Where the profile lives
docs.text:
A provider profile is team configuration, not code. The checkout ships defaults in <checkout>/src/cartridges/providers/; cox install points a new machine at claude-code.yaml there. A team keeps its own profile outside the checkout, in <home>/providers/ or in the workspace, with catalog.yaml beside it, and the machine profile's provider_profile names it:

# ~/.config/agent-tools/profile.yaml
provider_profile: <home>/providers/my-team.yaml

cox setup doctor fails its home paths row when provider_profile sits outside both <home> and the workspace. Every machine that runs lanes for the team uses the same profile, so the store it names is the same. See Install for the copy commands.

docs.title: The operator
docs.text:
The machine profile's operator key names the human the courier and decisions address. It lives in ~/.config/agent-tools/profile.yaml, not in the provider profile. Its default is operator, so a profile that omits it addresses "operator". Set it to a team role or a handle:

operator: reviewer-on-call

The settings command flags operator-only rows with the field operator_only. It also writes the older name pat_only with the same value, for one release, so use operator_only in anything new.

docs.title: Where the detail lives
docs.text: The shipped profile, src/cartridges/providers/claude-code.yaml, is commented key by key: tiers, classes, effort, budget_usd, role_budget_usd, role_ceiling_usd, tier_overrides, defaults and tools. Copy it and change what your team needs. Install: Providers lists the providers and their status.

docs.title: Several machines
docs.text: This page shows how to run Coxswain lanes on more than one machine, launch them from one place, and bring their work home to land. It assumes you have run Coxswain on one machine.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
The chair is the machine where you run cox. It keeps the workspace, which holds your tickets and task records. It also does all landing. Other machines only run lanes.

All machines share one run store. The store is a Postgres named by storage_url in the provider profile. Add the driver to cox with the postgres extra:

uv tool install --force --editable "<home>/installs/coxswain[postgres]"

<home> is the coxswain home, ~/.local/share/coxswain by default. The install replaces the extras cox had, so name each one you use, such as [postgres,lake].

With a local SQLite store, everything stays on one machine.

docs.title: Set up a lane machine
docs.text:
Do these steps on each machine that will run lanes.

  1. Install Coxswain as in Install. Also clone each repo your initiatives target, at the same absolute path as on the chair, with its .venv and check tools. The lane reads the initiative's repo: path unchanged.
  2. Install cox with the postgres extra, as above.
  3. Use the same provider profile as the chair. It is team configuration and lives outside the code checkout, in <home>/providers/ or the workspace; copy it there and point the machine profile's provider_profile at it. Its storage_url names the shared Postgres.
  4. Put claude on the PATH of a non-interactive ssh shell, and log in. Set a git user.name and user.email.
  5. Run cox setup doctor.

The store row of the doctor shows the store's kind and run count. It never shows the URL.

From the chair, cox setup doctor --host <name> also runs claude auth status on the host. It adds a claude auth row. The row reads like this when the login is good:

claude auth      ok

When it is not, the row reads like this, and the doctor exits 1:

claude auth: not logged in on the host (run claude auth login there)

Run claude auth login on the host. A login can lapse on a machine nobody types on, so a lane machine that worked last week can fail this check. cox route launch --on <host> runs the same check first and refuses to launch when it fails.

A login watchdog also checks every lane host's Claude login over ssh every 30 minutes, timing out after 60 seconds, and records the result with the host's beat. A host whose login has lapsed gets no new lanes; it stays in the hosts table and its running lanes continue.

docs.title: Name the lane machines on the chair
docs.text:
On the chair, list the lane machines in the routing profile:

lane_hosts:
  - {name: box2, ssh: user@box2, workspace_dir: /home/user/workspace}

workspace_dir is the workspace's absolute path on that machine.

ssh is a destination only. Put a port, user or key in your ssh config under a Host alias, and use the alias here. Connect once by hand so the host key is known.

Run the doctor on a lane machine from the chair with --host:

cox setup doctor --host box2

The doctor runs there over your own ssh config. The profile holds no keys.

docs.title: Add a host to the shared table
docs.text:
Add the host to the hosts table in the shared store so placement can fill it:

cox host add box2 --ssh me@box2 --capacity 3

--capacity is the lanes the host may run at once. An optional --weight sets its share of new placements, and an optional --capabilities names the list it can be matched on.

Once the table has rows, it decides: a host in the profile's lane_hosts but not in the table is not a lane host. cox host add and a launch with --on print a note naming such hosts. A launch takes the host's workspace from its own beat (cox host beat on that machine), else from the same-named lane_hosts entry. cox setup doctor --host reads only lane_hosts; cox host doctor box2 uses the table.

cox host drain box2 stops launching on the host while its live lanes finish; cox host activate box2 makes it a lane host again. cox host list prints one line per host: its state, capacity, beat age, and login.

docs.title: Launch a lane
docs.text:
Launch an epic on a lane machine with --on:

cox route launch epic --initiative work/<id> --on box2

The command allocates the run id on the chair. It copies work/<id> to the host with rsync. It then starts the lane there over ssh.

docs.title: Watch the lanes
docs.text:
The docket, cox route status and cox runs top list lanes that other machines hold. Each one reads like this:

<run> (on box2, since HH:MM, heartbeat Ns ago)

The docket is cox route context. Liveness comes from a lease in the shared store. A second run of the same epic is refused on any machine.

A lane counts as lost only when its host has gone quiet and its own lease heartbeat has been quiet for 10 minutes; a lost lane is marked lost and relaunched on another host. Placement weighs each host's weight and capabilities when it fills free lanes.

docs.title: Make a lane machine the resident chair
docs.text:
A lane machine can run the chair loop itself. cox chair service --install --host <name> prints the steps that put the loop on that host as a systemd user service; add --apply to run them instead of printing. cox chair service --status --host <name> reports it.

Two steps stay with a person: loginctl enable-linger and systemctl --user enable --now.

docs.title: Land the work
docs.text:
When the lane ends, bring its work home:

cox runs fetch <run>

This brings the lane's task records and log to the chair. It also fetches its branches, agents/<run>/*, and its phase branches, epic/<initiative>/*, from the host's repos, and the fetched run's approvals reach the ticket files. Then run cox runs land as usual.

The autonomous chair does the fetch itself. It runs cox runs fetch before it lands a remote lane.

The chair's copy of a ticket stays at its old state while the lane runs. The land marks it done.

docs.title: Shared storage
docs.text:
With no settings, traces live under runs/traces and the Iceberg lake under runs/lake on each machine. One machine needs nothing more.

For several machines, point traces_url and lake_url in the provider profile at a shared path. An NFS mount works, if every machine has it at the same absolute path. No new service is needed.

For object storage, use s3:// URLs with a self-hosted S3-compatible server, such as Garage. Add an object_store block to the provider profile:

object_store:
  endpoint: http://example.internal:3900
  region: garage
  access_key_env: GARAGE_ACCESS_KEY_ID
  secret_key_env: GARAGE_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
  path_style: true

The profile names the environment variables that hold the key and secret. It never holds the values. A literal key in the profile is refused. cox lake doctor shows the endpoint and whether each variable is set.

docs.title: A Garage server
docs.text:
A single-node Garage on the tailnet needs one profile block. Replace <host> and <bucket> with your own:

object_store:
  endpoint: http://<host>:3900
  region: garage
  access_key_env: GARAGE_ACCESS_KEY_ID
  secret_key_env: GARAGE_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
  path_style: true
traces_url: s3://<bucket>/traces
lake_url: s3://<bucket>/lake

Garage 1.1 also needs two SDK settings. Without them the pyarrow S3 client fails every upload with invalid checksum algorithm. Set both to when_required:

  • AWS_REQUEST_CHECKSUM_CALCULATION=when_required
  • AWS_RESPONSE_CHECKSUM_VALIDATION=when_required

Keep the key, the secret and these two settings in one env file. Write them as export NAME=value lines and set the mode to 600:

export GARAGE_ACCESS_KEY_ID=<key>
export GARAGE_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=<secret>
export AWS_REQUEST_CHECKSUM_CALCULATION=when_required
export AWS_RESPONSE_CHECKSUM_VALIDATION=when_required

chmod 600 <the EnvironmentFile path>

The file's path is the one cox chair service uses as EnvironmentFile. Source it from the login shell's startup file on every machine. For zsh that is ~/.zshenv:

. <the EnvironmentFile path>

Lanes started over ssh get their environment from that file and from nothing else. A file sourced only from an interactive startup file does not reach them.

A run reads the profile when it starts. It reads it again when it writes its trace at the end. A run started before the file existed fails its trace write with object_store names env var ... which is not set. The first trace in the bucket comes from the first run started after the change.

Check the setup in three places:

  • cox lake doctor shows the endpoint and whether both variables are set.
  • cox setup doctor has a traces row that names the endpoint.
  • The bucket listing shows a trace after one run.

Other URL schemes and cloud-specific sign-in come from plugins in the coxswain.storage entry-point group. The Plugins page lists the groups. Core names no cloud vendor.

Traces and the lake still stay local unless these are set.

docs.title: Land from any machine
docs.text:
By default the ticket files hold each task's state, which is work_state: files. When the provider profile's storage_url names a shared Postgres database that answers, the loop reads work items from the store instead; cox route status then prints work state: store first. A local SQLite store keeps the files as the board. Only the chair lands from the ticket files; any machine can land once the store is the board.

With the store as the board, a land on any machine checks that the task is approved in the store. It holds a lease named land:<task> while it merges. It moves the task to done with a compare-and-set. If another machine landed the task first, the land stops before it merges anything. The ticket file's state: is updated after.

The ticket files become a cache. After editing them by hand, cox route import writes them to the store, and cox route drift compares the two. This command also shows how they differ from the store:

python -m harness.store_cli regenerate-states <work_dir> --initiative <id>

Add --apply to rewrite their state: lines.

When the shared store already holds the lane's task records, cox runs fetch brings only the lane's branches.

Every machine that lands needs a checkout of the workspace. Ticket bodies stay in git.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: This page settles how a skill gets attached to the work: a skill binds to a role, and the skill's own body (not the role, not the binding) is the source of truth for what an agent in that role actually does.

docs.title: Two keys bind skills
docs.text:
A cartridge binds skills in two places:

  • skills: binds the roles a graph's nodes ask for (plan, build, review_charter, work_state_arm and so on) to one skill each. Base lists the roles under roles.required and roles.optional; a required role left unbound is refused at load.
  • crew: binds the seats a person delegates to (the crew members) to the skills they route to. It is optional. A seat with no binding routes to nothing team-specific.

A skill is named plugin:skill. The local cartridge, for example, binds:

skills:
  plan:           local-skills:plan-task
  build:          local-skills:build-in-worktree
  review_charter: local-skills:review-charter

The same skill can bind to more than one role, and in more than one cartridge.

docs.title: The skill body is the source of truth
docs.text: Everything a bound role does comes from the skill's own body: its instructions, its discipline, its description of what "good" looks like for that job. The role and the binding are plumbing that gets the right body in front of the right agent for the right run. If a skill's behavior needs to change, the fix is in the skill body, not in a role-specific patch layered on top of it.

docs.title: Where bindings and bodies live
docs.text: Bindings are cartridge keys, layered like any other: base binds nothing, local binds every required role, and a team overrides what it wants. The skill bodies Coxswain ships live in the checkout under src/cartridges/skills-plugins/ and move with its release tag. The harness also reads every folder named in the profile's skills_roots. See Cartridges for how provenance works.

docs.title: Writing a new one
docs.text: If no existing skill does the job, see Write a skill for the shape a new one needs and how it gets bound once it exists.

docs.title: Team cartridge
docs.text: This page settles how a team gets its own cartridge: run cartridge init <team>, then decide whether you're extending local or base.

docs.title:
cartridge init 
cartridge init my-team --cartridges-dir <workspace>/cartridges

This creates <workspace>/cartridges/my-team/ from the example team: a cartridge.yaml and a context/ folder for your charter and conventions. It links base and local beside it, pointing into the checkout's src/cartridges/cartridges/. It then prints the profile lines that name the new team. --extends base makes it extend base instead of local; --dry-run prints the plan and writes nothing.

It does not write your charter or conventions for you. Those are yours to write, because they say what your team actually believes.

The keys

A team cartridge's top-level keys are the same shape as base's: write kinds with their risk and ramp, policy, landing_areas, context, and a crew key naming which skills bind to which seats. Fragments under cartridge.d/ add to them; see Fragments. A team may not lower a risk or shorten a ramp that local or base set; see Cartridges.

Checks

landing_areas.checks lists the commands the harness runs on every build, as {name, cmd} entries, with an optional timeout (seconds) and fix (a command that repairs what the check found). A repository can add its own checks on top with a root .agent-checks file. See Landing.

The project layer

A repository can also carry .agent/cartridge.yaml. The harness reads it for runs against that repository and folds it in last. It may set only description, context, policy.review_tier, policy.cost.level and landing_areas.checks. Its checks list replaces the team's list for that repository; .agent-checks still adds to it. Any other key is refused.

The project layer may only tighten review: it may lower a review_tier threshold, add to tier2_surfaces and remove from tier0_patterns, never the reverse. It may move policy.cost.level toward strict, never toward liberal.

Extending local or base

Most teams extend local (the default) rather than reaching past it to base. Extend base directly only when your change is genuinely independent of anything local has already decided; reaching past a layer that already narrowed something usually means you're fighting the layer instead of using it.

What lands where

A team cartridge doesn't replace base or local; it's resolved on top of them at run time, layer by layer. See Fragments for how the pieces inside your cartridge are folded, and Policy for the values most teams change first.
Write a graph
docs.text: This page settles the shape a new graph needs, where it goes, and how a run picks it up.

docs.title: The shape
docs.text:
A graph is the ordered set of nodes a run executes, with a DAG of real dependencies between the tasks it schedules — see Graphs for what a node and an edge mean. A new graph is a new course, not a new node: writing a new node type (a new kind of review, a new kind of validation) is a different, larger change than composing existing node types into a new order.

In code, a graph is a module with a function run(args, runner) -> dict. It reads its cartridge and date from args, asks the runner for roles and tiers, never skills or models, and returns proposals as data. It writes nothing. src/graphs/docs/GRAPH-CONTRACT.md lists the rules, and tests/test_portability.py in src/graphs enforces them.

docs.title: Where it goes
docs.text:
A graph is a module under src/graphs/graphs/delivery/ (work that produces work) or src/graphs/graphs/ops/ (keeping a running system honest). The module opens with a docstring that names the node chain right under its title line, such as decompose -> adversary -> emit; the diagram on the graph's docs page is generated from it by python -m harness.graphdoc. The module declares GRAPH_NAME and a module-level SPEC, a graphs._spec.GraphSpec naming the subcommand, the run function, a one-line summary and the Needs that become command-line flags.

Graphs are platform code. They live in the coxswain repository, not in a team cartridge, and a new one lands as a pull request there.

docs.title: How a run picks it up
docs.text:
Discovery is automatic. harness/registry.py imports every module under graphs/ and collects each SPEC, so a new module is a new shell.py <subcommand> with no dispatch table to edit. Two names clashing is an error, not a silent shadow.

Reaching it from cox is not automatic:

  • cox route launch starts a fixed set: epic, decompose, rescue, cos and sweep.
  • The coxswain dispatch graph can select only graphs its driver, harness/cos.py, knows how to build arguments for (_KNOWN_GRAPHS). A new graph joins dispatch by extending that list and its argument builder.

docs.title: What to check before writing a new one
docs.text: A new graph is worth writing when an existing one's phases and edges don't fit the work — not when a single task in the middle needs different handling. A task that needs a different review tier or a different budget is a Policy change; a task that needs different nodes entirely, in a different order, is a new graph.

docs.title: Write a skill
docs.text: This page settles the shape a new skill needs, where it goes, and how it gets bound once it exists.

docs.title: The shape
docs.text:
A skill is a body of instructions for one job: what a builder does, what a charter reviewer holds work to, what a validator checks. It describes discipline and judgment, not a script: the agent filling the role still reasons about the specific task, using the skill body as its brief. See Skills for how the body becomes the source of truth once it's bound.

The file is SKILL.md, with a short front matter:

---
name: plan-task
description: Turn one work item into an ordered, bounded plan another agent can execute without asking questions.
---

# Plan

You produce the plan for exactly one work item...

docs.title: Where it goes
docs.text:
A skill lives in a plugin: a folder with .claude-plugin/plugin.json (which carries the plugin's name) and a skills/ folder. Each skill is skills/<skill>/SKILL.md, and its bound name is <plugin>:<skill>:

my-skills/
  .claude-plugin/plugin.json      {"name": "my-skills", ...}
  skills/
    review-data/SKILL.md          -> my-skills:review-data

Keep your team's plugin in your workspace, beside your cartridge, and add its folder (or the folder holding it) to the profile's skills_roots. The harness scans each root for plugins. The skills Coxswain ships are in src/cartridges/skills-plugins/local-skills/.

docs.title: How it gets bound
docs.text:
Bind it in your team cartridge, under skills: for a graph role or under crew: for a seat:

skills:
  review_charter: my-skills:review-data

The cartridge loader refuses a bound name that resolves to no body, or to more than one. Resolve the cartridge to check:

cartridge --team my-team --cartridges-dir <workspace>/cartridges --skills-root <path> --json

Writing the skill and binding it are separate steps: the skill can exist and be versioned before any cartridge binds it.

docs.title: What to check before writing a new one
docs.text: A new skill is worth writing when no existing skill's body actually covers the job, not when an existing skill's body could be edited to cover it too. Editing an existing skill changes it for every role and cartridge that already binds it; writing a new one doesn't.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Coxswain is one package, coxswain, and one command, cox. Install cox, then let cox install set up the rest.

brew install ppfenning/coxswain/cox          # or: uv tool install --python 3.14 coxswain
cox install --team my-team
mkdir -p <workspace>/work <workspace>/runs <workspace>/intake <workspace>/cartridges
git -C <workspace> init
cartridge init my-team --cartridges-dir <workspace>/cartridges
cox setup doctor

<home> is the coxswain home: --home, else COXSWAIN_HOME, else $XDG_DATA_HOME/coxswain, else ~/.local/share/coxswain. <workspace> is <home>/workspaces/main unless you pass --workspace.

When the home has no checkout, cox install clones one at the release tag matching its own version into <home>/installs/coxswain, then reads manifest.toml from it. That checkout is the whole install: there is one, with one venv.

The doctor that cox install runs at its close may report the missing workspace and cartridge until the mkdir, git init and cartridge init steps are done.

docs.title: Getting cox
docs.text:
Homebrew (macOS, and Linux with Homebrew):

brew install ppfenning/coxswain/cox

Current Homebrew refuses a formula from a third-party tap until you trust the tap. If it does, run brew trust ppfenning/coxswain once and install again. The formula also installs towpath, the dashboard.

The formula carries no optional extras. After brew install and after every brew upgrade cox, run cox setup extras. It installs traces, parquet, lake and postgres into the venv cox runs from, at the versions this release's uv.lock pins, and pip checks the sha256 of every wheel. Without it cox setup doctor reports that the store needs psycopg. --with EXTRA ... picks a subset and --dry-run prints what would be installed. When the extras are already present at the locked versions it says so and changes nothing.

uv:

uv tool install --python 3.14 coxswain

uv must already be on your PATH; get it from https://docs.astral.sh/uv/. The --python 3.14 flag makes uv fetch a 3.14 interpreter when none is present. Add the extras the machine uses, for example uv tool install --python 3.14 'coxswain[postgres,traces,lake]'. A shared Postgres store needs postgres. The extras are traces, postgres, parquet, lake, analytics and live; cox install keeps the ones the tool already has. If your shell cannot find cox afterwards, run uv tool update-shell and open a new shell.

docs.title: What cox install does
docs.text:
1. Reads manifest.toml in the checkout of ppfenning/coxswain at <home>/installs/coxswain. It refuses a checkout with uncommitted changes, and refuses a --provider that the manifest does not mark supported. A clean checkout is installed as it is; moving it to another release is cox upgrade's job.
  2. Creates one venv in that checkout, <checkout>/.venv, with uv sync.
  3. Installs cox editable from the checkout, so cox and the harness run the same code.
  4. Writes the profile for this machine, ~/.config/agent-tools/profile.yaml, when it has none: harness_dir is <checkout>/src/graphs, skills_roots is <checkout>/src/cartridges/skills-plugins, and provider_profile is the shipped default, <checkout>/src/cartridges/providers/claude-code.yaml. See The provider profile for pointing it at your team's own.
  5. Links the crew seats from <checkout>/crew into ~/.claude/agents.
  6. Fetches dash when you pass --with dash. Dash is the only optional component; it lives in its own repository.
  7. Runs cox setup doctor. It also checks that the --provider CLI (claude by default) is on PATH.

docs.title: Channels
docs.text: Channel The checkout follows Command release the release tag vYYYY.M.N cox install edge main cox install --edge

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Run cox install --help for the flags your version accepts. The ones this page uses:

Flag Meaning --team Which team's cartridge the profile names. --workspace The workspace the crew works in; <home>/workspaces/main by default. Required with --root. --home Absolute path of the coxswain home, used when --root is omitted. --root Use the checkout at <root>/coxswain instead of <home>/installs/coxswain. --provider Which provider in manifest.toml to install for; claude-code by default, and only a supported one is accepted (see Providers). --with dash Also install dash (towpath). --edge Follow main instead of the release tag. --dry-run Print the plan and change nothing.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
cox setup doctor

cox setup doctor checks the checkout, its venv, the profile and the home, and that the configured provider's CLI is on PATH.

docs.title: What you'll see
docs.text:
cox versions lists the checkout's release, and dash's tag when dash is installed, against manifest.toml.

cox setup doctor against a real install.

docs.title: The provider profile
docs.text:
A provider profile is team configuration: which CLI drives the seats, the model, effort and budget for each tier and role, the tools each role may call, and the shared store and trace locations (storage_url, traces_url, lake_url, object_store). The checkout ships default profiles in <checkout>/src/cartridges/providers/, and cox install points this machine at claude-code.yaml there. That is enough for one person trying Coxswain.

A team keeps its own profile outside the code checkout, so cox upgrade never touches it and the checkout stays clean. Put it in one of two places:

  • <home>/providers/<team>.yaml, one copy per machine;
  • the workspace, for example <workspace>/providers/<team>.yaml, so it travels with the workspace's git history.

Start from the shipped one, and copy catalog.yaml beside it (prices are read from the catalog.yaml next to the profile):

mkdir -p <home>/providers
cp <home>/installs/coxswain/src/cartridges/providers/claude-code.yaml <home>/providers/my-team.yaml
cp <home>/installs/coxswain/src/cartridges/providers/catalog.yaml <home>/providers/

Then set provider_profile in ~/.config/agent-tools/profile.yaml to that path, or pass --provider-profile PATH to cox setup install. The doctor's home paths row fails when provider_profile sits outside both <home> and the workspace.

Personal setup never goes in the code checkout. It lives in three places:

  • The team cartridge, in <workspace>/cartridges/<team>, holds the cast, the policy, the inline repos and the context packs.
  • The provider profile holds the tiers, budgets, tools and the store.
  • The machine profile, ~/.config/agent-tools/profile.yaml, holds this machine's paths, the forge and tracker, the operator (operator:) and the notifier (notify:).

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text:
Update cox itself, then the checkout:

brew upgrade cox            # or: uv tool upgrade coxswain
cox upgrade

cox upgrade moves the checkout to the newest release tag (or --to VERSION), syncs its venv, reinstalls cox from it with the extras it had, relinks the crew, moves dash if you have it, and runs the doctor. It refuses a checkout with uncommitted changes.

docs.title: Moving from 0.47 or earlier
docs.text: A machine installed with 0.47.0 or earlier has a checkout per component. Move it to the one-checkout layout with cox setup migrate; see From 0.47 to the monorepo.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
There is no cox uninstall yet. Remove cox with brew uninstall cox or uv tool uninstall coxswain, then delete the coxswain home (or --root) by hand.

See Supported machines for prerequisites on specific platforms.

docs.title: Supported machines
docs.text: Every platform below needs git and curl before you run the installer. Coxswain needs Python 3.14 or newer; uv downloads a managed Python 3.14 when the system one is older, so you don't need to install it yourself. Install uv itself first, or install cox with Homebrew.

docs.title: Arch and Omarchy
docs.text: git and curl are in the official repos: pacman -S git curl. Omarchy ships both by default, so on a stock Omarchy install there is nothing to do before running the installer.

docs.title: Debian and Ubuntu
docs.text: apt install git curl covers the prerequisites. The system python3 is usually older than 3.14, which is fine: uv downloads its own.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text: git ships with the Xcode Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install). curl is preinstalled. uv downloads Python 3.14 if the system one is older, or install it with brew install python@3.14.

docs.title: Proxmox LXC
docs.text: Use an unprivileged container with a current Debian or Ubuntu template, and follow the Debian and Ubuntu prerequisites above. Nesting isn't required — the installer doesn't need a container runtime, just the two prerequisites and network access to GitHub.

docs.title: Docker clean room
docs.text: For a disposable, fully isolated install, run the installer inside a container built from a Debian or Ubuntu base image with git and curl installed. This is the fastest way to try Coxswain without touching the host machine at all.

docs.title: What you'll see
docs.text: cox install --dry-run prints the plan cox install would run, before it writes anything.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
A provider profile tells cox which CLI to drive and what each crew tier and role may spend and call. manifest.toml's [providers] table lists the providers. cox install --provider <name> (default claude-code) checks the name against that table and checks that its CLI is on PATH; the profile it writes always names the shipped src/cartridges/providers/claude-code.yaml.

Provider Status What the profile supplies Claude Code supported The claude CLI on PATH, and the per-tier model, effort and budget ceiling for each seat. Codex planned A profile still needs to name the Codex CLI on PATH and map Coxswain's seat tiers to Codex's own model and budget controls. Gemini planned A profile still needs to name the Gemini CLI on PATH and map Coxswain's seat tiers to Gemini's model and budget controls. local experimental providers/local-oss.yaml declares the capabilities the harness reads and maps the cheap tier to a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with standard and deep still on Claude; no runner drives it yet, so the install works only as a declaration.

Only Claude Code is installable today. cox install --provider refuses any other name: provider 'codex' is 'planned', not supported.

A team's own profile lives outside the checkout, in <home>/providers/ or the workspace; see The provider profile.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: This page settles why the platform is shaped the way it is: work moves in small tasks, review is blind by design, a claim needs the check that proves it, and a budget is a shape constraint rather than a slider to turn up.

docs.title: Small tasks
docs.text: One ticket is one unit of work with one pull request. If a task needs three PRs, it was really three tasks, and splitting it earlier is cheaper than untangling it in review. A ticket that hasn't been scoped goes to a future-work area, not onto the active board — scoping is what promotes it.

docs.title: Blind reviewers
docs.text: A charter reviewer checks a change against the team's written standards. An adversary reviews the same change without seeing the charter reviewer's verdict, looking for what the charter reviewer missed. Neither sees the other's conclusion first, because a reviewer who already knows "this passed" reviews differently than one who doesn't. See Review for how the two verdicts are arbitrated into one.

docs.title: Evidence over assertion
docs.text: A proposal that asserts something is true carries the check that proves it: a command and its output, not a recollection. Absence of an error is not evidence of success — a job that reports success while writing nothing has not succeeded. See Records for what gets kept as evidence, and where.

docs.title: Budgets as shape constraints
docs.text: A budget is not a number to raise when a task runs over it. The rule is split, never raise: a task that needs more than its ceiling allows was too big for one task. See Budgets for the ceilings themselves and what a stop records.

docs.title: The rest of this section
docs.text: Crew and seats says who does the work. Cartridges says how a team's own standards get layered in. Graphs says how a run is put together. Landing says how a run's change reaches a human.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.text: This page settles what a budget is for: a per-node dollar ceiling by tier, enforced by one rule — split, never raise — and a record of exactly what happened when a task hit its ceiling.

docs.title: Ceilings are per node, by tier
docs.text:
Every node in a graph (plan, build, review and the rest) has a dollar ceiling for its session. The provider profile sets it: budget_usd per tier (the Claude Code profile: cheap $0.15, standard $0.35, deep $0.80), and role_budget_usd for roles that need a different number, such as the reviewers. The ceiling is a property of the node and the tier, not something a single run negotiates for itself.

A build is the exception that proves the rule. Its budget is a guide for one slice, not a ceiling for the task. The guide is estimated from the repository's recent builds, clamped to $1.00 to $4.00. At the guide the harness judges go or no-go; a build that passes resumes. The provider profile's role_ceiling_usd (the Claude Code profile: build $6) is the failsafe on the build's cumulative spend. See Autonomous chair.

docs.title: Split, never raise
docs.text: When a task is going to exceed its ceiling, the answer is not a bigger number. It is a smaller task. A task that needs more budget than its tier allows was too large for one task, the same way a ticket that needs three pull requests was really three tickets. Raising the ceiling to fit the task hides the signal that the task should have been split before it ever ran.

docs.title: budget_usd on an item
docs.text: A work item can carry its own budget_usd. It replaces the estimated build guide for that item. It may be higher than the estimate, but never higher than the cartridge's build_budget_usd_max (base: $6). The harness refuses an item that asks for more and quotes the cap. See Policy.

docs.title: What a budget stop records
docs.text: When a node hits its ceiling, the run stops there rather than continuing on credit. What gets recorded is the amount spent against the ceiling, the node that was running, and the task it was working — enough for a human to see whether the task needs splitting or the ceiling needs revisiting for that tier generally, as a policy change, not as an exception for one run.

docs.title: Cartridges
docs.text: This page settles how a team's own standards enter a run without forking the platform: a cartridge layers base, then local, then team context, in fragments that only ever tighten what came before.

docs.title: Three layers
docs.text:
A cartridge is a packaged bundle of context for a team or a repo: its conventions, its charter, its thresholds. It resolves in three layers, applied in order:

  • base — the substrate's own conventions and epic model, the same for every team.
  • local — whatever this repository has already layered on top of base.
  • team — the specific team's own charter and thresholds, added last.

Each layer names its parent with extends:, and the chain is merged parent-under-child. A repository can add a fourth, narrow layer of its own, .agent/cartridge.yaml; see Team cartridge.

Each layer can add to or narrow what the layer below it says. None of them can lower a risk or shorten a ramp.

docs.title: Fragments live in cartridge.d/
docs.text: A layer is its cartridge.yaml plus any fragments in cartridge.d/*.yaml, folded in sorted order after it. A fragment has the same keys as cartridge.yaml; a later value wins a scalar conflict, so the file name is part of the contract. Prose (a charter, conventions) lives in markdown files named by the context: list, which concatenates base-first: a team refines a base principle, it does not replace it. See Fragments for how a team edits its own.

docs.title: Tighten-only
docs.text:
Two fields carry this rule: a write kind's risk (how dangerous the write is) and its ramp (how many clean runs before the harness stops asking). A child layer or fragment may raise the risk or lengthen the ramp; it may never lower either, and the loader refuses the resolve if it tries, naming the layer or fragment file.

The loader enforces this for risk and ramp, and for a few other rules at load time: every required role is bound, every bound skill resolves to exactly one body, every context path exists. Other values (budgets, review tiers, landing_areas.checks) merge child-over-parent, so a team sets its own; a team's checks list replaces the one it inherits. Keeping risk and ramp tighten-only is what makes layering safe to compose: a reviewer reading the base pack still knows the floor every team stands on for what a write may do without a person.

docs.title: The skills and crew keys
docs.text: A cartridge's skills key binds the roles a graph's nodes ask for (plan, build, review_charter and so on) to skill bodies. Its crew key binds the seats a person delegates to. Together they are the mechanism Crew and seats describes generically, made concrete per team. See Skills.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
The base and local cartridges ship inside the coxswain checkout, under src/cartridges/cartridges/. A workspace's cartridges/base and cartridges/local are links into that folder, so they move with the checkout's release tag. A team does not edit them in place.

Every fragment a run assembles can be traced back to the release that shipped it. A team pack that wants something different extends base or local (see Team cartridge); it does not patch the shipped cartridges directly.

docs.title: Crew and seats
docs.text: This page settles who does the work: the crew are the agents, each one filling a seat with a role and a set of skills bound to it, and the coxswain is the one component in the loop that dispatches without ever building.

docs.title: The crew rows, the coxswain steers
docs.text: The crew are the agents that plan, build, review, and validate a task. The coxswain dispatches work to them and enforces the in-flight bound — the cap on how many runs are active at once — but it never fills a seat itself. If the coxswain built, reviewed, or validated, it would be marking its own work, and the review that follows would have nothing independent left to check against.

docs.title: A seat is one role, one job, one run
docs.text: A seat is one role in the crew filled by one agent doing one job on one run: builder, charter reviewer, adversary, arbiter, validator. A seat does not carry state between runs — the next run starts a fresh seat, even if the same provider profile fills it.

docs.title: Skills are bound, not baked in
docs.text: A seat's behavior comes from the skills bound to it for that role, not from anything hardcoded into the seat. The skill body is the source of truth for what an agent in that seat actually does; the seat is just the slot. See Skills for how a skill gets bound to a seat and a role.

docs.title: One writer per board
docs.text: Exactly one component is the writer of any given board or state machine. If two seats could move the same ticket, the board's state would be a race, and nobody could reason about what it means. Every seat other than the single writer proposes; the writer applies.

docs.title: Where a seat's context comes from
docs.text: A seat's prompt is assembled from fragments — pieces of context text layered in by cartridge, not written into the seat itself. Change the fragment and every seat that reads it changes with it; change the seat and something structural has changed instead.

docs.title: Graphs
docs.text: This page settles what a run actually executes: a graph is a course laid out in advance — phases, tasks, and a DAG of edges that are real dependencies, not just the order someone happened to write them down.

docs.title: A graph is a course
docs.text: A graph is the ordered set of nodes a run executes: plan, build, review, arbitrate, validate, and so on. It is defined once and reused by every run, the way a rowing course is laid out once and rowed by every crew that races it.

docs.title: What a graph may not do
docs.text:
A graph owns sequence. It decides which node runs next and what each one is asked. It writes nothing at all: no file, no branch, no pull request, no ledger row.

Every consequence belongs to the harness instead — the worktree a build runs in, the checks that have to pass, the gate a write goes through, and the append-only ledger that records what happened.

The split is what makes a new graph cheap. Write one and it inherits the gate, the worktree, the checks and the ledger by existing, rather than by remembering to call them. It also bounds what a bad graph can cost you: the worst it can do is ask for the wrong thing in the wrong order, because it has no way to touch the repository at all.

Two more names finish the picture. A cartridge says who a run works for — which skills a role uses, which model a tier gets, where a write is allowed to land. A runner executes one node against a provider and returns what it said. Swap the runner and the same graph runs against a different provider; swap the cartridge and the same graph works for a different team.

docs.title: Phases order tickets that need it, and only those
docs.text: An epic is a container with one section per phase. Phases are ordered; tickets within a phase are not necessarily. A dependency edge belongs between two tickets only where order genuinely matters — a dependency that exists because a task "feels sequential" blocks work that could have run in parallel for no reason.

docs.title: Tasks are the DAG's nodes
docs.text: A task is one unit of work: one ticket, one pull request. The DAG's edges run between tasks, and an edge that isn't a real dependency shouldn't exist — it costs the docket a slot that could have dispatched something else.

docs.title: Run ids and worktrees
docs.text: Every execution of a graph against a task gets a run id, so the record for one attempt never gets confused with another attempt at the same task.
